This paper explores the emergence of a dual methodology, under which program assertions comprise declarative statements within a formal language. Based on the mathematical structure of this language, assertions are translated into formal statements, and their validity is evaluated through a semantic analysis. This paper examines the methodology's core principles, its application to programming languages with complex features, and the use of model checking to validate assertions. The methodology is also adapted for Markov decision processes and probabilistic logic. Ultimately, this paper delves into the potential advantages of incorporating this theory of assertions within existing formal verification tools. We present Unet++, a next-generation modular, multi-scale modular deep neural network designed for traffic forecasting at various prediction horizons. Comprising a central encoder-decoder block with residual connections and parallel convolutions, as well as adaptive skip connections, this architecture builds on the Unet architecture. It modulates the feature maps through weighted summation of the skip-layers, enabling preservation of spatial information while adapting to prediction tasks. Additionally, the Unet++ architecture incorporates the SE block to enhance feature representation by identifying inactive feature maps, and employs dilated convolution to increase receptive fields and reduce parameters. We adapt the ResNet architecture to create the Central-Net, Encoder-Net, and Decoder-Net modules within Unet++. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SummAss, Waymo, and BDD-100K datasets, demonstrating scalability and efficiency. Moreover, the Unet++ architecture is capable of handling a wide range of input data, including occluded images, as seen in the BDD-100K dataset. This makes it an ideal solution for real-world traffic forecasting applications. Code is available at https://github.com/SORElab/Unet++./tree/master. We contribute this architecture in the form of a submission to the CVPR 2022 traffic forecasting challenge. Due to the early stages of the pandemic, we submitted the work in March 2021, but it remains largely unpolished until now. A more detailed description of the approach can be found at https://sorelab.github.io/article/unetplus. We also present a detailed analysis and discussion in the accompanying article published at Journal of Image and Graphics Technology (JIGTE), under the title 'Analyzing Modularity in Deep Neural Networks: The Unet++ Story'. A supplementary video is available at https://sorelab.github.io/article/unetplus-video. We utilize the JAX library, initially called jax.pytorch, to develop the model, utilizing the default PyTorch library, and the ADABOUND library by first-hand contributor Yang Yu, under the pseudonym 'xaxa64'. Our approach leverages the PyTorch optimizer, evaluating the performance on the test datasets, including SummAss, Waymo, and BDD-100K, due to the lack of access to the corresponding test datasets. A pre-trained model is available at https://sorelab.github.io/article/unetplus. The research is supported by the grant 20-2031 from the Czech Ministry of Education

We examine the precategoral rewriting system concept, which expands existing theory to incorporate partial functions and precategories, precosets, and precodes adapting notions of substitution, pattern matching, and reduction. This system is defined by small, weakly-finite families of partial functions with specified domains and codomain precosets. The development involves interpreting Rewringing Graphs in a precategoral setting and demonstrating that a rewriting system is coherent if it meets the precategoral analogue of the single-step congruence criterion, leading to the Coherent Rewringing Graphs Theorem. Furthermore, we prove that a precategoral rewriting system is stably finite if it meets the precategoral analogue of the stable single-step congruence criterion, resulting in the Stable Finite Rewringing Graphs Theorem. Additionally, we introduce the concept of precategoral computability, establish a finality criterion for rewriting systems, and show that the precategoral framework encompasses both functors and computable functions as special cases. Lastly, we discuss the precategoral framework's implications on the development of programming languages and call for the incorporation of partiality and possibility in language design. The well-established toolkits of List-Processing and Functional Programming provide a solid foundation for incorporating the concepts presented here, along with the novel precategoral abstractions introduced. The formalism and computational analysis provided in Appendix A through J have been formally verified using the Coq proof assistant, supported by the Agiri Coq library. The approach chosen for the paper's content reflects the objectives of Agiri and the Agiri Coq library, which prioritise the promotion of novel computational concepts through the development of verified participatory programming frameworks. The contributions of the paper are as follows:

- Introduce the concept of precategoral rewriting systems, expanding existing theory to incorporate partial functions and precategories, precosets, and precodes.
- Prove the Coherent Rewringing Graphs Theorem, demonstrating the precategoral rewriting system's congruence criterion.
- Prove the Stable Finite Rewringing Graphs Theorem, establishing the precategoral analogue of the single-step congruence criterion.
- Introduce the concept of precategoral computability and finality criterion for rewriting systems.
- Show that the precategoral framework encompasses both functors and computable functions as special cases.
- Discuss the implications of precategoral analysis on programming language design and the incorporation of novel abstractions.
- Verify the paper's content using the Coq proof assistant

A reliable hippocampus segmentation is of utmost importance in updating anatomical automatic segmentation algorithms to account for changes caused by hippocampus resections due to epilepsy surgery, thus ensuring metric accuracy. Although recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved hippocampus segmentation, it remains unclear if these improvements extend to cases with hippocampus resections. In this research, we assessed the effectiveness of recent 3D and 2D models in segmenting resected and non-resected hippocampus, and found that current methods were less accurate when applied to resected hippocampus cases, with a notable drop of around 20-30% in performance. Notably, our study revealed that a T1-contrast based approach outperformed other methods by segmentation Dice score, and showed more consistent results (around 60% lower loss) compared to other automatic segmentation methods when applied to resected hippocampus cases. Our analysis also highlighted the value of incorporating T1-contrast in training models to better learn hippocampus features. Overall, our findings suggest that a T1-contrast based approach may serve as a more reliable method for updating anatomical automatic segmentation algorithms and achieving accurate and consistent results in cases with and without hippocampus resections. The developed model, HippoT1, has demonstrated promising performance, and we recommend its use in improving long-term segmentation consistency. The code for HippoT1 is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ManoelVonMendi. Our study's segmentation results have achieved high scores of 0.874 and 0.863 (respectively for training and testing data) using the Dice score metric. Our study's alignment metrics showed even better results, with a mean target deviation of 1.547 mm and 1.731 mm for volumetric differences. Notably, our study's findings have been accepted at the 27th International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI 2024). Notably, our study's findings have been further validated by expert manual correction, resulting in an improvement from 72.3 to 91.1 in terms of Dice score, and from 10.3 to 4.9 in terms of mean target deviation. Our findings illuminate the delicate balance between path and traversal degrees of freedom, underscoring the necessity to accommodate a trailing edge in alignment when sampling traversal states, thus enabling access to normally hidden fringes due to mode overlap. Cosmic rays entering the Earth's atmosphere initiate a series of interactions that eventually lead to the production of protons. This process occurs when a primary cosmic ray (such as a high-energy nucleus) collides with an atmosphere molecule, resulting in the creation of various secondary particles. If one of these secondary particles is a charged hadron, it can continue interacting with other molecules, producing more secondaries. This cycle of particle production continues until the resulting particles have sufficient energy to escape the atmosphere, primarily consisting of protons at this stage. These escaped protons then constitute the galaxy's cosmic ray flux that is detected by Earth-based and space-based observatories. Additionally, secondary neutrinos are produced during these interactions, contributing to the expected neutrino flux from the atmosphere. This study focuses on analyzing the production of these secondary protons and neutrinos, taking into account the influence of the atmosphere's finite height and spatial geometry on particle production. Comprehensive simulations of cosmic ray interaction in the atmosphere have been conducted using three distinct Monte Carlo methods: Pythia 8, Sibyl 2.3, and Lunds 98, comparing their results with data from previous studies and neutrino flux predictions from atmospheric models. A novel algorithm was developed to calculate the cosmic ray flux at Earth's height from atmospheric production, expressed as an energy-dependent production function. This production function compares the expected atmospheric neutrino flux with present-day observations, showing a 20% discrepancy with current data for 100 MeV energy neutrinos, a 30% discrepancy for 500 MeV neutrinos, and a 40% discrepancy for 1 GeV neutrinos. Further analysis of high-energy production (at least 10 GeV) also shows that the atmospheric neutrino flux at Earth's height would be increased by 30% if the atmosphere's geometry were to be accounted for beyond standard production models. Consequently, this expected flux enhancement contributes up to a 10% rise in the atmospheric production component of high-energy neutrinos, predominantly affecting the high-energy neutrino flux's energy dependence. Recently, the importance of topological structures in artificial neural networks has been recognized, and several studies have been motivated to develop novel skeleton representations. This paper proposes a novel skeleton representation called PyraSkeleton. It's derived from a pyramidal structure, comprising multiple sub-graphs of varying node densities. This configuration offers flexible and efficient representations for both training and inference phases. PyraSkeleton can be learned by differentiating it from PyraAlphaSkeleton, an adaptable and trainable skeleton representation, thus bypassing the need for additional spatial pooling layers. Experiments have been conducted on the CIFAR-10 dataset using ResNet as the baseline, resulting in PyraSkeleton-based networks demonstrating improved generalization and parameter efficiency, equivalent to the application of spatial pooling methods, while allowing the architecture to remain unaltered. Additionally, PyraSkeleton has the added benefit of preserving crucial information for inference. This representation provides a new perspective on the interplay between topology and spatial structure in deep neural networks. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengxilo/PyraSkeleton. Our PyraSkeleton-based models have achieved superior performance on the ImageNet dataset, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art. The models can be accessed at https://github.com/singulareti/diplommatia2/tree/master/PyraSkeleton-ResNet. Furthermore, the implementation of the first fully differentiable skeleton representation, PyraAlphaSkeleton, has been optimized using adjoint calculus, thus enhancing its adaptability and differentiability. This approach specifically defines a predicate domain that accounts for both data and control flow constraints. The abstract interpreter uses a Galois pair, where the abstract domain approximates the precise set of Hoare triples, and the concrete domain represents the inverse relationship. The proposed abstract interpreter is demonstrated to be a sound approximation of the precise Hoare triple set. Enforcing neighborhood fairness in graph representation learning has become a topic of interest due to its potential to improve task accuracy through reduced bias.  However, the traditional definition of neighborhood fairness is challenging to apply in real-world scenarios because it relies on strict definitions.  A notable issue is that neighboring nodes are often unfair by nature.  To address this limitation, a new definition of neighborhood fairness is proposed, referred to as the extended definition of neighborhood fairness.  This definition is more flexible and applicable in various graph-based learning tasks.  The proposed definition is based on a concept called the B-nearest neighbors of a set of nodes, where B is a variable integer.  For instance, when B is 1, the B-nearest neighbors become the traditional neighbors.  To measure the extended definition of neighborhood fairness, a new metric called extended graph fairness (EGF) is introduced.  EGF calculates a lower bound on the expected task loss conditional on a given node's label when considering a given node's B-nearest neighbors.  To create a fair model, a new maximum-EGF optimization problem is formulated, which aims to find a node's representation that maximizes the expected task loss conditional on its label given its B-nearest neighbors.  This optimization problem can be solved using a variety of approaches, such as semidefinite programming or convex box constraints with an optimization black box.  To address the extended definition of neighborhood fairness, a new approach called extended 1-Neighborhood Fairness (1NF*) is proposed.  1NF* enforces neighborhood fairness when B is 1, which is a simplified version of the extended definition of neighborhood fairness.  The proposed approach is evaluated using real-world node-labeling data from two graph representation learning tasks, where it is demonstrated that 1NF* outperforms traditional approaches like Graph Convolutional Networks and Invariant Graph Convolutional Networks.  Interestingly, 1NF* is shown to be a more effective approach than Invariant Graph Convolutional Networks, which suggests that enforcing neighborhood fairness through the invariance principle may not always be effective. Currently, data synthesis is a common approach to address data scarcity for code-switching tasks, yet it remains unclear whether the extent of synthesis impacts the quality of acquired data. We investigated this by dividing synthesized data into three categories based on increasing intensity, utilizing two code-switching languages: CSW and ASW. We found that English sentences serving as the base for data synthesis undergo an average of 24 word replacements in the most intense category. Notably, we observed fewer than half of the replaced words contained the correct code-switched form, highlighting the negative effect of excessive synthesis on data quality. To validate our findings, we compared real and synthesized data within the framework of a few-shot training regime, revealing that reducing synthesis intensity leads to enhanced performance. We discovered that replacing only individual words instead of segments, with minimal segment replacement, optimizes our model's results, achieving 23 F or 24 F metrics depending on the training dataset. Interestingly, we found that the few-shot training regime consistently outperforms extensive synthesis-based training. We hypothesize that this may be due to excessive synthesis producing unnatural code-switching phrases with extended consecutive code segments, ultimately hindering model performance. Building upon this knowledge, we developed an automated data refinement tool to rectify poor synthesis, enhancing data quality and, in turn, model performance. We investigate these geometries as separate entities and in relation to each other within an interbrane picture. Both perspectives prove valuable. We explore the characteristics of individual branes within a background field and how they adapt when embedded in a background undergoing a smooth transition from high to low energy states. We examine the interbrane interactions within a collective perspective. We also use the interbrane picture to derive brane properties from duality constraints. A mesh's overall effectiveness is measured by how accurately its individual components function. In this research, a novel approach is developed to rapidly assess and improve meshes consisting of connected elements, such as tetrahedral cells in 3D space. This method focuses on the local reliability of each mesh element and uses data from nearby areas to determine its trustworthiness. Our approach combines a flexible, mesh-dependent assessment tool with a refinement strategy that aims to perfect the accuracy of each cell by recasting it from the most reliable surrounding areas. Several adaptive mesh optimization techniques are also proposed, such as prioritizing cells based on predicted error rates or selecting and merging potential cell combinations in advance. We introduce a novel algorithm for efficiently constructing new, high-quality meshes from lower-quality ones by identifying and combining highly reliable cells. Our approach is validated through various numerical tests, including simulations of incompressible fluid and elastic material flows, which demonstrate the significant potential for mesh improvement and resulting accuracy gains. Additionally, the results show that the increased complexity of the resulting meshes may offset any benefits in terms of computational efficiency. Furthermore, a new measure is proposed to balance the trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency for meshes refined using the proposed strategy. This measure is based on the concept of information gain and is used to assess the effectiveness of different mesh refinement techniques. We also present a novel algorithm for efficiently splitting and creating new cells in the process of mesh refinement, which significantly improves the computational performance of the system by reducing the repeated calculation of costly functions associated with the local element splitting process. This algorithm is shown to provide comparable results to the previously published method by Siegerbauer, but at a substantially improved time complexity of O(n (l+1/2)3/2) as opposed to O(n (l+1)3/2). Our approach was successfully applied to a real-world scenario in the field of nuclear engineering, where it was used to improve the accuracy of a mesh used for simulating elastic material flows. The resulting improved mesh was then used to simulate a severe accident scenario at a pressurized water nuclear reactor and the results showed a significant 57% reduction in the predicted evacuation time for the surrounding area. Offline reinforcement learning in large continuous spaces is challenging, particularly when using the current optimal action approximation. This approximation often leads to a focus on near-optimal actions and neglects less effective ones, hindering the learning of more distant actions. Existing policies typically stick to previously learned actions near the optimal ones, failing to explore further. We address this issue by refining the concept of smoothness in action space to enable policies to easily transition between actions close to or far from the optimal ones. Our SmoothOpt policy leverages this revised smoothness by sampling actions based on the balance between near-optimal actions and those far from them. Additionally, we enhanced the variance reduction in OptMMD to integrate both state and action values into the objective function. We demonstrate that our approach achieves better results on practical problems in comparison to the original OptMMD. The new objective allows for better learning along optimal policy trajectories, and incorporating both state and action values promotes smooth action transitions. We confirm that our method outperforms alternatives through successful demonstrations. Furthermore, we found that our technique significantly reduces task failure rates, and one of our models even achieves zero failures, making it transferable to new tasks without failure as well. We provide additional insights into our findings and offer practical tips for task success. The code is available at https://github.com/zermeling/SmoothOpt. We also presented the results at the 4th Workshop on Efficient Machine Learning (EffML) 2021.

One of the main obstacles to applying Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to real-world scenarios is achieving empowerment-based transferability, which enables one agent to facilitate another agent in completing a task. Empowerment measures an intervention's ability to increase the target variables' entropy, indicating its potential to enhance uncertainty and problem-solving options. However, empowering other agents typically requires agents to deviate from optimal task-solving policies and instead focus on helping, which may hinder task completion. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning models often adopt the collaborative distillation approach, where agents learn from each other to improve task performance. We explore the idea of distilling empowerment as a means of transfer, developing a novel optimization method in the process. This method leverages the maximum empowerment of optimal joint actions, enabling agents to focus on helping without compromising task efficiency. We also propose a decentralized algorithm to tackle scalability issues, which we evaluate in simple scenarios and find it outperforms existing alternatives. Additionally, we analyze the algorithm's convergence and provide empirical analysis to understand the relationship between empowerment and helpfulness. Furthermore, we show that our optimization method for maximum empowerment is NP-hard and adapt a graph algorithm to approximate this optimization under certain conditions. This approximation has a polynomial time complexity and can be implemented in the online setting but may not always achieve the exact maximum empowerment. With this approximation, we establish a connection between empowerment and helpfulness and find a positive correlation between them. Lastly, we discuss possible future research directions involving the concept of empowerment. These directions include integrating this concept with metrics like success or return to provide more comprehensive and practical transferability between collaborative agents. Moreover, customizing agent tasks to facilitate empowerment-based transfer could be another interesting area of study. In addition, exploring the relationship between symbiotic learning and empowerment might provide novel insights, especially if symbiotic learning proves to be a more efficient mechanism of transfer. Lastly, incorporating the concept of empowerment into the online setting, particularly in dynamic environments, could be another interesting area of study. For the sake of conciseness, we will refer to maximum empowerment as empowerment henceforth. Each scale is treated as an independent network, and features are aggregated through a convolutional layer to generate multi-scale objects. The traditional methods used to assess magnetic fields, like the Milne circle and radial field, are based on specific spatial arrangements of magnetic data that consider fill factors to maintain solenoidality. Recent findings have established that considering magnetic fill fraction can improve the accuracy of magnetic field assessments. The Spherical Harmonics decomposition offers a framework to integrate fill factors, but applying this method is complicated. To build upon the existing understanding of magnetic field assessments, we developed new formulas for the harmonic coefficients of various magnetic field models that account for fill factors. This involves decomposing fill-gaps into small areas and assigning magnetic values to them. We introduced a new concept, called fill fraction geometry, to describe the geometry of fill-gaps and developed algorithms to compute their areas. The new formulas mark the first attempt to incorporate fill factors into magnetic field symmetry decompositions. They show that accounting for fill factors modifies symmetry decompositions in specific ways. For instance, in models like the Milne circle and radial field, the modified decomposition resembles the original one scaled by the fill fraction. The new formulas allow us to compute the harmonic coefficients of fill-gapped magnetic field assessments, which can be used in vector magnetic field projections. To showcase their accuracy, we compared projections based on traditional and fill-gapped symmetry decompositions, showing that the fill-gapped approach produces more accurate results when the fill fraction is considered. This new framework provides a comprehensive understanding of magnetic field symmetry decomposition and can be used to develop projection methods for practical applications. Three metrics for evaluating complex words within the English language have been
linked to distinct aspects of language complexity: 1) morphological depth with
word internal structure (Morfix), 2) semantic breadth with word scope (Semfix),
and 3) phonological density with sound quantity (Phonfix). Previous studies
linked each measure to separate aspects of language variability. We aimed to
investigate the connections between these word-level metrics and typological
features at the sentence level. We calculated the relationships between the
morphological measures Morfix and Semfix, as well as the phonological measure
Phonfix, and various linguistic characteristics such as word order, case systems,
and grammatical relations, using a database with 65 languages. We discovered that
the morphological measures related most strongly to case systems and grammatical
relations, while the phonological measure was linked to word order. Notably, we
found no connections between the semantic measure due to its limited applicability
to the included languages. These findings suggest that while a language's
morphological characteristics might reveal its typological features, there is no
straightforward link between word-level metrics and structural properties at the
sentence level. Nonetheless, morphological complexity was found to have the most
robust connections to multiple aspects of language variability. We hypothesize that
this connection stems from the overlap between word-level and sentence-level
complexity in morphological features. We propose that this type of indirect link
could explain the relationships observed in our study. Additionally, we suggest
that future studies explore the connections between word-level and sentence-level
complexity using advanced, data-driven approaches. The results of our study could
have implications for understanding language acquisition processes, particularly
for second language learners who often face difficulty with complex words. The
findings might also provide valuable insights to linguists studying language
acquisition, processing, and comprehension. Ultimately, our research may contribute
to the development of more effective language processing algorithms by considering
the morphological complexity of English words. The data and code utilized in this
study are openly accessible at https://github.com/alejoc/fixedpoints.

Our results reveal that the performance of reduction heavily depends on the chosen observation operator, and not only provides a straightforward approach but also a strategy for selecting optimal observation points. Furthermore, the technique's applicability is demonstrated through noise tolerance in the example cases. Two practical scenarios – a Cahn-Hilliard equation and wave equation – are used as platforms to evaluate the reduction method's effectiveness, and the approach is potentially adaptable to scenarios with multiple parameters without significant computational difficulties. Our findings also indicate that the technique's performance can be further enhanced by incorporating Monte Carlo sampling based on optimal observation points. Two significant paradoxes in the foundations of quantum mechanics, Frauchiger-Renner's and Hardy's setups, are shown to be resolved by applying the quantum version of Bayes' rule, which also addresses the quantum twins scenario. The analysis utilizes two simple mathematical tools: a functional for mixed states and a diagrammatic representation of composite systems. The solution to the paradoxes is achieved by assigning specific probabilistic meanings to various participants in the setups. Specifically, it has been necessary to consider the quantum information processing perspective on Hardy's scenario. Furthermore, it has been found that implementing the Hardy scheme for validating a mixed-state preparation requires an explicit specification of the source's probabilistic output distribution, which is not required in the context of classical information processing. The reconciliation of the results is attributed to a distinct interpretation of the term 'quantum probability'. It has also been found that a frequentist interpretation of the results of quantum processes cannot be applied without violating classical logic without causing inconsistencies, which are, however, avoided when the quantum Bayes' rule is used. (The final version of this article is already published in an journal, whereas this statement refers to the arXiv preprint version.)

This article explores boundary conditions at infinity in 2D Euclidean scalar field theories when applied to a given cutoff. Unlike standard Dirichlet boundary conditions, periodic boundary conditions cause a shift in the field phase by 2π upon entering a new cell, leading to a twofold ambiguity in defining these theories. A case study involving massless Gaussian free field demonstrates that the periodic theory's phase is determined by the number of cells, not the field's initial values. A partial proof and rigorous analysis are provided, along with a demonstration of multiple periodic theories in the field theory's standard superstructure, involving a shift in phase multiple times. A related argument suggests that these non-trivial theories exhibit a shift in phase equal to 2π times the number of cells when entering a new cell, but the rigor of this claim depends on resolving a significant mathematical question regarding the non-triviality of these theories. It is suggested that the phase ambiguity of these theories could be resolved by viewing them as limits of theories defined on finite but infinitely subdivided lattices. Finally, speculations are made about the potential extensions of these findings to theories involving non-abelian symmetries, such as QCD. A thorough examination is conducted to verify whether these theories could exhibit a non-trivial infrared fixed point, leading to a more concrete understanding of their properties. A mathematical question arises regarding the relative importance of the various periodic theory fixed points, and it is hypothesized that the standard theory may be the sole fixed point under certain conditions or the most prominent one in the process of lattice refinement. A final question is posed regarding the possibility that the phase ambiguity of these theories could be resolved by viewing them as limits of theories defined on finite but infinitely subdivided lattices. A brief discussion is also provided on how these findings might be quantified using lattice gauge theory simulations and an analysis of the potential extensions of these theories to other classes of symmetric theories. A comparison is made with theories defined with different boundary conditions at infinity, such as the theory of charged periodic states discovered in a recent study. A possible extension is considered of these findings to theories defined with different types of boundary conditions, such as the theory of charged periodic states discovered in a different study. A final discussion is provided on how these findings might be quantified using simulations for a class of theories defined with mixed boundary conditions, such as the theory of massless QED. A possible extension is considered of these findings to theories defined with mixed boundary conditions, such as the theory of massless QED.

Most image search algorithms face difficulties with identically transformed copies due to transformations like compression, which can arise from various methods such as retouching software or network delays. The problem of detecting near-copies is particularly challenging, as a thorough solution would need to offer equivalent results to exact matches. The proposed Active Indexing technique enhances image detection by integrating transformation functions into indexing tools, allowing for faster and more accurate identification of images and their transformations. By utilizing a fast search algorithm that allows for a limited number of queries, Active Indexing significantly outperforms existing solutions in image copy detection. Active Indexing's effectiveness was demonstrated through experiments comparing search time and false positive rates using various transforms on multiple image datasets. Results show that Active Indexing achieves a 10-fold improvement in search time while maintaining a transformed accuracy of 99% and only a 1% increase in false positive rate. In the entity typing task, specific mentions within sentences relate to particular fine-grained categories, such as "city" or "organization." While early efforts on entity typing focused on identifying suitable mentions for typing, later studies incorporated mention encoding networks to gather relevant information. Nash Equilibrium is a critical concept in economics where multiple entities determine their actions based on strategies to achieve a stable equilibrium. Predicting this equilibrium is crucial, but traditional approaches based on fixed point optimization or neural networks often struggle with efficiency or flexibility. To address these issues, we propose the Nash Fixed Point Network, a novel and adaptable architecture capable of handling various game scenarios by combining modular design and feature augmentation techniques. Experimentation on a diverse dataset shows N-FPN's superiority over both baseline models and a leading generative adversarial network approach, while we also provide access to open-source implementation for others to build upon. 

Key contributions of our work include:
1.A new neural network architecture, the Nash Fixed Point Network, designed for Nash Equilibrium prediction through modular learning.
2.A comprehensive dataset collection, known as the NFGD, for game-theoretic experiments containing diverse games and larger populations.
3.N-FPN's performance comparison with both baseline models and a leading GAN approach on the NFGD dataset demonstrates its effectiveness.
4.Open-source code availability for replication and potential integration with other architectures, enabling others to build upon our work. 

The code is available online at https://github.com/azazzaa/nash-fixed-point-network. 

In the remainder of this document, we describe the proposed architecture, present findings from N-FPN's evaluation, discuss implications and potential future directions, and share our implementation details. 

Section 2 introduces the proposed Nash Fixed Point Network architecture and its design rationale. 
Section 3 outlines the evaluation process, including the dataset used, N-FPN's training, and performance comparison with baseline models and a leading GGN approach. 
Section 4 discusses limitations, potential future directions, and implications of our work. 
Section 5 describes the implementation details of N-FPN. 

Throughout this document, we aim to contribute not only the proposed architecture, but also the larger NFGD dataset, showcasing a broader range of games and population sizes, to advance research in this field.

In our study, we found that EvoCrash tends to overlook crashes caused by method invalidation. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach, InvalID, that identifies methods likely to become invalid after modifications. InvalID then induces such method invalidations during mutation testing, which requires developers to fix the issue. By integrating InvalID, we created two new mutation testing tools: (i) a tool that increases the number of failures, including those caused by method invalidation, and makes them more similar to real failures; and (ii) a tool that minimizes artificial failures, including those caused by method invalidation, and prioritizes locating the original failure. resulting in a noteworthy observation: speaker (sp) data exhibits a stronger 
orientation in the event plane than antiparticle (asp) data, leading to a range 
of asp/speaker ratios below one. This speaker-asp dichotomy is shown to be 
sensitive to the speaker's movement within the event, emphasizing the importance 
of correctly isolating speaker and asp information. Additionally, we find that 
the ratio of v_2 for speaker/asp to v_3 for speaker/asp is an effective indicator 
of whether the speaker's movement is consistent with fluid dynamics or was influenced

investigations of speaker/asp ratios across various collision energies and

speaker/asp ratios below one dominant at higher energies and the opposite at

properties by examining speaker/asp ratios across multiple collision systems

in resolving current discrepancies and finding the speaker's movement's 
connection to fundamental system properties, potentially opening new areas 
for theoretical and experimental research into the speaker's movement.

pure asp data, allowing us to compare asp data with a variety of other collision 
systems and find speaker/asp ratios below one across a broad energy range.

Concept location involves pinpointing the sections of the code related to a particular concept, usually a term extracted from a developer's query or requirements documents. This study focuses on enhancing concept location through training, relying on thousands of annotated examples gathered from numerous software projects on popular repositories like GitHub and Stack Overflow. We created a training dataset of 1,523 actual conversations and 1,523 fabricated conversations, each with five sentences, by manipulating the language model's prompts. We selected 12 distinct words and replaced them with 12 possible alternatives for each prompt, resulting in 12 different possible conversations for each set of prompts. We then used Neural Enertainment Distance (NED), a metric that measures the distance between two conversational models, to identify artificial conversations. During testing, NED achieved a 75% accuracy across different conversational topics, including, sports, politics, and, fiction. Visual understanding of human actions is a vital aspect of AI research, yet challenging to segment due to ambiguous action boundaries.  Existing Action Parsing algorithms rely on detailed annotated action videos, which are scarce, making generalization difficult.  We present a novel method to improve performance on action segmentation tasks by leveraging co-occurrence information.  Our approach, called Co-occurrence Action Parsing (CAP), employs a two-stage model architecture.  First, individual body parts are predicted in terms of overall actions and co-occurring actions.  We then refines these predictions by incorporating co-occurrence information.  Our CAP model outperforms previous methods on UCF101-24 and HMDB51 datasets, achieving stronger action segmentation performance with less complex architecture design.  CAP model also demonstrates effective generalization to novel actions on Dataset2Action, a benchmark for video action recognition.  Our CAP source code is available for public use at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/ CAP.  This repository includes all model designs, training, evaluation, and data visualization tools.  We will provide the CAP model with pre-trained weights for UCF101-24 and HMDB51 on the AliResearchOpen GitHub repository.  Our research is open to collaboration and contributions. Automated feedback is given to students by Grader; it shares its evaluation of their code alongside the instructor's feedback on their test attempts. A two-year experiment involving over 600 students from 14 classes across three universities examined the impact of various forms of Grader feedback. The results indicate that providing code coverage as a metric, along with overall grades and feedback from the instructor, has a positive effect on student performance: they write more tested code and receive higher grades. Notably, covering all relevant test cases becomes a primary focus for students when this information is shared with Grader. Interestingly, providing the instructor's feedback and Grader's code review are less crucial factors in determining student outcomes. A follow-up survey found no significant connection between students' perceptions of Grader and their performance. Consequently, university administrators and instructors may feel more comfortable disclosing Grader's code to students due to its limited influence on student behavior. A proposed modification to sharing Grader information, known as the "sensitive threshold," could potentially revive its role in supporting student learning. Ultimately, the experiment's findings suggest that providing students with instructor feedback and code review is most effective when doing so directly. Despite this, sharing Grader information with students may help reduce instances where instructors choose not to provide feedback. A new survey found that nearly a third of university instructors decline to give feedback to their students. Consequently, a policy of only sharing Grader information in response to instructor feedback from university administrators may help alleviate this issue while still allowing students to see Grader's code in courses where instructors are willing to provide feedback.

We introduce a neural network architecture that leverages prior knowledge of detector conditions in experimental particle physics. This design incorporates a customizable graph structure, where a node's influence is adjusted based on detector factors, such as position and orientation. The architecture's first layer uses a variable topological structure influenced by detector features, that adapt to the underlying physics signatures. The graph's subsequent layers maintain the characteristics captured in the input phase, where each node's influence is adjusted to account for background and signal fractions in different detector regions. The architecture's validity is demonstrated by implementing it in the search for a long-lived top squark in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, specifically in the decay of top squarks into leptons, where it shows notable improvements over standard convolutional neural network methods. The implementation details of this novel network architecture are discussed, along with the associated computational challenges and solutions. The development of this architecture relies on the understanding that a neural network can learn and represent key properties of a process even when its structure is intentionally constrained to retain only the most relevant information from detector variables. The network's performance is evaluated in terms of reconstruction performance and sensitivity to signal and background rates. The graph-based architecture's unique properties are explored through various signal and background scenarios. The implementation of this novel neural network method is seen as a promising approach to exploiting detector information in high-energy physics experiments. The method may be applied to other search channels and analysis areas, such as data validation and consistency checks. The technique may also be adapted for use in other scientific fields that involve multi-dimensional data collection. The associated code is publicly available on the CERN CERNARH repository at https://github.com/cernph-susy2017-top. The research findings were presented at the 2017 Top and SUSY Tools workshop in CERN. In optimal control for partially observable environments, a problem closely related to asset pricing can be interpreted as solving for the stochastic process that minimizes cost subject to beliefs-based constraints. A type of neural network, the recurrent neural network, can be used to find an approximate solution. By viewing the neural network's hidden states as beliefs for various state variables, we show an equivalent formulation that reflects the constraints directly in terms of these hidden states. A new type of loss function is then introduced, resulting in a two-player game dynamics that mirrors reinforcement learning. This leads to a novel algorithm, Eagle, which approximates the solution by iterating between two stages: one optimizing the hidden states and the other projecting the hidden states to satisfy the constraints. Eagle is implemented in Python and is available for download at the reference link. The algorithm's performance is evaluated in the context of a financial model based on a hidden Markov model. The results, including minimal constraint violations, are shown to be comparable to a direct method with the additional benefit of faster computation at larger sizes. The algorithm's performance is also compared to reinforcement learning methods, such as Deep Recurrent Q-Networks, with the advantage of being a general solution that can handle optimal control for a partially observable state. The algorithm's potential for solving a variety of optimal control problems is further demonstrated in the supplementary materials with additional models, one based on a linear Gaussian system and the other based on a mixed environment. The results show Eagle's ability to recover the true stochastic process in the ideal case and achieve minimal constraint violations in the practical case. Our proposed method, ATTC, combines actor-text-correlation with graph convolutional networks to predict action detection in videos.  ATTC consists of three key components.  First, it uses actor-role-relationship to identify actor-roles from video transcripts and represents actor-roles through word and motion embeddings. The paper investigates a particular heat equation in a domain characterized by a unique shape anomaly: a reentrant corner. This analysis focuses on solving the associated initial-boundary value problem under both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, which yields a time-dependent harmonic function. Employing a combination of classical methods and stabilization techniques, the problems are decomposed into more tractable forms. Specifically, the work draws on theories involving the representation of solutions to second-order parabolic equations, the extension of the solution to a related elliptic equation, the use of two-sided estimates for the solution, and the properties of the Dirichlet heat kernel. By leveraging these approaches, the paper establishes a detailed understanding of the solution, including its rate of decay as time approaches infinity. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the solution tends towards a time-stationary equilibrium when that equilibrium exists. Interestingly, the solution exhibits a different behavior when its time-stable state exhibits an oscillatory pattern. Specifically, the work shows that this equilibrium acts as the generalized limit of the solution's time evolution, which remains bounded in a specific norm even as time approaches infinity. This behavior gives rise to a continuum of Dirichlet and Neumann orbits, which are invariant under the long-time dynamics and comprise functions that are continuous on the domain's interior while discontinuous on its boundary. Importantly, the results obtained generalize and improve the existing results for the case where the boundary conditions are uniform and the domain has a single corner. Additionally, the work offers novel insights into the behavior of solutions to the heat equation in bounded domains with mixed boundary conditions. Specifically, the results show that these solutions exhibit a universal behavior not previously documented in the scientific literature. Importantly, the work bypasses the need for specialized techniques drawn from the theory of spectral analysis and instead relies on a novel approach to obtaining two-sided estimates for the solution based on its extension to a related Dirichlet problem. Furthermore, the work shows that this approach allows the solution to be extended in a controlled manner while remaining consistent with its original norm. In the process, the work obtained a generalized version of the solution's representation that complements the existing results for the case where the boundary conditions are uniform. Importantly, the work demonstrates that this representation remains valid even when the solution exhibits jump discontinuities on the domain's boundary. Additionally, the work offers a generalized version of the solution's representation as an integral of the heat kernel weighted by the solution's initial values, which may be viewed as a parabolic analogue of the classical representation

The use of Graph Neural Networks has led to significant advancements in table structure and content extraction from complex document images. Given that standard GNNs often focus on identifying distinct entities as nodes, a major limitation arises from the difficulty in building comprehensive graphs that can capture interconnections among extracted tables, cells, and lines. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel, end-to-end approach that employs a GNN-based graph construction and table top-down inference framework. In this method, each graph node is assigned a detailed label, indicating whether it represents a complete table, cell, or mere text line. This distinct labeling enables the development of a tailored GNN-based computation, graph construction, and table inference process. Furthermore, our approach incorporates a GNN-based decoder that predicts table structures and content based on the labeled and constructed graph. Notably, the end-to-end approach allows the GNN to learn and optimize the graph construction, simultaneous node labeling, and table recognition processes in a single, unified training process. Consequently, this method can identify tables accurately, character recognition is performed on these tables, and the resulting table content is organized in a semantically sound manner. Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on the ICDAR 2019 Table Challenge dataset, achieving 77.9% F-score for table structure identification and 63.1% F-score for table content extraction. The implementation details of our approach can be found on GitHub at the specified link. Additionally, we introduce a distinct set of characters, including superscript and subscript characters, based on the ICDAR 2019 Table Challenge dataset, which contains 215, 114, and 77 characters, respectively. The end-to-end approach has significantly enhanced cell and cell line extraction accuracy, achieving 83.0 F-score for cell structure identification and 51.4 F-score for cell content extraction compared to the baseline methods. The F-score for line identification is 74.7. Moreover, our approach has successfully demonstrated its ability to generalize on real-world document images through a comparison with a dataset of real document images, achieving a mean F-score of 65.62. The inferred tables from real document images match the actual tables in the data up to 93.22% in mean similarity score. The ultimate goal of research in Game of Life studies is to identify high-level strategies from a vast ruleset.  In contrast, this paper examines how games of varying sizes are influenced by rule variations, focusing on a basic aspect - location counting.  Through an extensive survey, experts were asked to categorize locations as essential or irrelevant for winning the game at different levels of complexity.  These categorizations were made without consideration for the game's solution, resulting in three distinct categories of location understanding: face recognition at the highest level, partial face recognition in intermediate levels, and no face recognition at the lowest level.  It was observed that lower-level players are more likely to be aware of face types than higher-level players, and also tend to make winning moves a game size or larger in advance.  These findings indicate that high-level understanding of the game is achievable without needing to analyze all locations, and knowing which locations are crucial for winning is a challenge primarily manageable by lower-level comprehension.  This distinction highlights the intricacies between these two levels of comprehension and suggests they may require different analytical approaches to understanding the game.  In addition, while many locations have no clear understanding, they are often characterized by simple patterns, and it is hypothesized that breaking these patterns down into their components could help bridge the gap between these two levels of comprehension.  If successful, this could lay the groundwork for a step-by-step breakdown of the game's rules, and ultimately unlock a general algorithm for solving the game.  However, this initial study is just the beginning and more surveys are needed to confirm these results and advance this hypothesis.  In the future, it's also anticipated that this distinction could lead to a more nuanced understanding of Glider Collision Paradox, a fundamental aspect of the Game of Life, and may ultimately provide a new perspective on the game's solution. Currently, clustering algorithms are limited to relatively small input sizes due to exponential time complexities. We propose a quantum K-means algorithm, the first of its kind, which can perform clustering tasks with multiple data sets of $n$ points in $d$-dimensional space in $O(d^2 + n)$ time. This algorithm's underlying query operations allow us to efficiently compute relevant mathematical expressions, essentially offering a faster way to compute multiple cluster-related quantities. We show that this algorithm's performance is inherently linked to the capabilities of the Hartigan-Kreweras invariant, but structurally it is associated with the more efficient Edelsbrunner's algorithm for nearest neighbor search. When tested on random data sets, the output of our quantum algorithm matched the results from the classical Edelsbrunner algorithm. Furthermore, the quantum approach also outperformed its classical counterpart in various practical tasks like data visualization and quantum clustering. We successfully applied the quantum K-means for tasks such as segmenting images and assigning quantum state labels. Its potential applications also extend to the analysis of quantum states. Although initially designed for use with a quantum computer, the algorithm's time complexity makes it a competitive alternative for use with classical data sets of size $n \lesssim 10^4$. When executed multiple times on random input data, the quantum algorithm yielded consistent results, but with some slight variations in the centre points at a rate of $O(2^{-d/n)$. We present a theoretical explanation based on the principles of quantum randomness and speculate that this error might be reducible with the use of a sufficient number of iterations. We also show that this error rate can be comparable to that of the classical algorithm under specific conditions. Finally, the code for this algorithm is publicly available at https://github.com/bruno-bp/quantum-kmeans. We believe the quantum approach has significant implications, not just for clustering tasks, but also for our understanding of clustering itself, and highlights interesting similarities and differences between quantum and classical data analysis methods. This study compares the operator experience of two Telepresence Robots, InVia and GoWest, which differ in their visual and navigation capabilities. A survey was conducted with InVia operators after 6 months of use, revealing significant insights into the distinct aspects of the robot's behavior and its impact on operators' interactions. Notably, operators expressed difficulty in adapting to changes in the robot's behavior, particularly sudden transitions in its navigation style. They also appreciated the visual enhancements provided by the robot, which allowed them to focus on their tasks rather than paying attention to the robot's movement. However, the robot's visual and navigation aspects often conflicted, leading to confounding experiences for the operators. A new framework has been developed to design the user experience of telepresence robots from the operator's perspective, incorporating three key components: transparency, consistency, and user engagement. This framework is essential for ensuring that interactions between the robot and operators are harmonious and efficient during operations. A proposed design framework is demonstrated using the InVia robot as an example, illustrating its application in telepresence systems. A notable outcome of this study is the identification of the operator's expectation of consistency in the robot's behavior as a fundamental aspect of the user experience. This expectation surpasses the desire for engagement, highlighting the need for designers to prioritize consistency in the robot's behavior, embracing it as a vital aspect of the user experience. A theoretical model based on the operator's expectations is developed, providing designers with a framework for balancing consistency and engagement to optimize the user experience. A concept called 'user experience overshoot' has also been identified, where excessive consistency can lead to boredom, and optimal user experience is achieved at a specific point between these extremes. A theoretical diagram, known as the user experience balance diagram, is designed to capture the delicate equilibrium between consistency and engagement. A notable insight from this study is the identification of navigation and control aspects of the user experience as distinct from visual aspects. A deep user segmentation has been identified, with three user segments exhibiting varying priorities among these aspects: a segment prioritizing visual aspects, another prioritizing control, and a neutral segment indifferent to visual aspects but highly engaged with control. A design strategy is proposed, addressing the needs of each segment individually. As designers strive to optimize the user experience, they must consider the distinct preferences and priorities of their target audience, shaping the user experience to accommodate their unique needs and desires. Mafia is a multi-player murder mystery game where hidden faction members engage in deceitful behavior, providing a key example in studies of rational deception. This research presents a mathematical framework for analyzing Mafia game dynamics and assessing its ending outcomes. An exhaustive investigation of the game's initial stages is carried out, focusing on the subsequent developments. Based on the findings, a probabilistic model is proposed to predict the game's final outcome. Factors influencing the game's dynamics and outcomes include the number of players, the number of murders, the reliability of allies' accusations, the reliability of the game moderator's accusations, the prevalence of ghosts, and the activities of the ghosts. In addition to deriving mathematical expressions for the associated probabilities, numerical calculations are performed to determine the expected outcome. A representation of the expected winner-to-ally ratio is also presented. This study's methods could be applied to other hidden action games, similar to Mafia. Several possible variations of the Mafia game are explored, including two variants that retain most of the game's characteristic features, but differ from the original game. These variants are found to have relatively small effects on the expected outcome. Finally, a simulation-based validation of the proposed mathematical framework is conducted to confirm its accuracy. Simulation results show a relatively small discrepancy between the estimated probabilities and the simulation-based estimates, ranging between 0.01 and 0.26 in some cases. Despite some discrepancies, the proposed framework demonstrates strong alignment with the simulation results, indicating its appropriateness for analyzing the Mafia game. The effectiveness of black-box models can be assessed through the use of conformal prediction, offering a way to derive prediction intervals for outcomes. This method is particularly relevant when predicting rare events, such as outcomes from medical imaging and radiotherapy treatments. This tutorial will cover the application of conformal prediction to black-box models, focusing on rare event prediction. Firstly, we will examine conformal prediction in its initial and expanded forms, examining its use with white-box and black-box models. Next, we will discuss recent advancements, including boosting, sequential, and conformal transformers, prior to concluding with future research directions and potential areas of future exploration. Our results show the potential for conformal prediction to significantly improve the evaluation of black-box model predictions, such as predicting tumor response to radiotherapy, with prediction intervals derived from model results enabling the comparison of predictive abilities of diverse models. Our code and data are publicly available for review at https://github.com/jrmgoring/conformal-prediction. A Boltzmann machine's complexity is quantified by its dynamic parameter space, which is investigated in detail. It is found that this complexity follows an power-law relationship with the size of the network, specifically for the dimensions associated with the adjacency matrix and bias vector. This power-law behavior holds true across various Boltzmann machine versions, including symmetric and asymmetric, directed and undirected, as well as those with and without self-loops. Moreover, the exponents governing this power-law are influenced by the type of algorithm used for training the network. An alternative measure of complexity is also proposed and found to yield comparable results. This newly devised metric offers a condensed representation of the dynamic parameter space, ultimately providing a means to identify and organize algorithmically generated solutions. By employing this metric, it becomes feasible to determine which fractions of the dynamic parameter space are accessible or inaccessible across varying network sizes. This study provides crucial insights into the dynamic parameter space of Boltzmann machines and sheds light on the inherent limitations of algorithms used to generate solutions. Furthermore, this work may also serve as a foundation for investigating the dynamic parameter space of other machine learning models. Interestingly, it appears that current algorithms are inadequately equipped to explore an increasingly substantial fraction of the dynamic parameter space as network size grows in proportion to the number of nodes, N. Specifically, this shortfall arises from an exponentially decreasing gap in accessibility, proportional to 1.5^N. This unfortunate imbalance means that an exponentially growing fraction of the dynamic parameter space remains unexplored with each additional node, leading to potential machine learning solutions that remain undiscovered. This study offers a compelling case for the development of more sophisticated algorithms to tackle larger-scale Boltzmann machines in the future. Although this analysis focuses specifically on Boltzmann machines, it is anticipated that similar investigations on other types of neural networks may reveal comparable or even more pronounced imbalances between accessible and inaccessible regions of the dynamic parameter space. To this end, the results presented here form a crucial foundation for future research in this area. Furthermore, this work offers a novel and significant contribution to the field of complex systems, offering an in-depth exploration of the dynamic parameter space of Boltzmann machines. By combining advanced analytical and computational methods, this study provides an exhaustive characterization of the dynamic parameter space, systematizing an intricate and complex domain. Automating the analysis of blood test results has the potential to greatly
enhance the healthcare industry's efficiency. To accomplish this, researchers must
develop techniques for identifying multiple related diseases using a comprehensive
patient profile. This requires analyzing inter-connected disease nodes in an
igraph graph, which can be solved by formulating the problem as a Markov
process and applying a dynamic programming method for optimization. We propose
a new IRLS-based approach to calculate the inferred probability distribution and
evaluate its performance against various scenarios using synthetic and real-world
datasets. The comparative evaluation of our proposed method against existing
solutions further validates its effectiveness. The source code for this method is
available for public access at https://github.com/multiome-team/BloodDiseases.

We develop an approximating variational method and provide specific variational parameters that minimize the error in the adiabatic Hamiltonian.  This minimization is contingent upon the norms of commutator stacks with respect to the adiabatic Hamiltonian.  Should the norms be small, our parameters yield an improved approximation of the adiabatic Hamiltonian, one that is equivalent to the initial variational approximation proposed by Li, Lu, and Zhang but with reduced complexity.  When the norms are large, our parameters yield a new approximation scheme that is distinct from Li, Lu, and Zhang's but also results in a broader applicability of the initial parameters.  Li, Lu, and Zhang's original work established parameters based on specific assumptions regarding the initial phase and Floquet-Bloch states. We suggest a model with radiative electroweak symmetry breaking and light electroweak doublet fermion ports that also serves as a feasible theoretical framework for dark matter. In this model, a 125 GeV Higgs boson is generated through double portal radiative symmetry breaking, and a separate sector of electroweak doublet fermions contributes to the inclusion of dark matter. The proposed fermion is a color-singlet fermion with a mass smaller than the electroweak scale and is stabilized through an approximate $U(1)_X$ symmetry. The model presents a common origin for both dark and visible matter particles. The model incorporates on-shell dark matter annihilation channels involving light electroweak doublet fermions, which helps to meet the relic abundance requirement. Additionally, the model allows for a feasible connection to the (g-2)_\chi of the dark matter particle. We thoroughly examined the model's properties and found that it can be distinguished from other theoretical models through LHC experimentation, specifically in the event of discovering new particles at masses of up to a few hundred GeV. This model also has implications for the understanding of the dark matter particle. If the approximate $U(1)_X$ symmetry is near to being an exact one, the model predicts the existence of a light Higgs boson with a mass of around 70 GeV. This model can be further constrained by future Dark Matter searches at the collider and in particle physics experiments. We explore the nonlocal features of realistic local hidden variable theories, which include Kochen-Schwartz, Gleason, and Fine theorems as fundamental components. We discuss the process of quantifying nonlocality using correlation distillation, which involves transforming local correlations into nonlocal ones by adjusting the measurements. The distillation process relies on the concept of quantum entanglement, along with the principles of superdeterminism if applying quantistic nonlocality as a solution. We analyze the Bell experiments' role in verifying nonlocality, along with the challenges posed by superdeterminism, while highlighting the importance of practical applications in understanding nonlocality. We conclude by discussing the nonlocal features of specific quantum systems, including transverse momentum entanglement, Bell's teleportation, and hybrid entanglement. We also explain how nonlocality manifests in hybrid quantum systems composed of different particles, including gauge and gravitational fields. Furthermore, we explore the concept of hybrid entanglement and nonlocality through a detailed examination of Bell's scenario, involving two photons generated in different experiments. We discuss the potential applications and practical feasibility of nonlocality in hybrid quantum systems, along with the crucial role of contextuality in understanding nonlocality. Lastly, we outline future research directions in investigating nonlocality in hybrid quantum systems, along with the need to address the difficulties inherent in nature.

This research focuses on developing algebras of slice over weighted graphs. We use the underlying graph's matrix algebra and tensor algebra to construct these algebras, providing equivalent interpretations in terms of path algebra and quiver mutation. Building on previous findings that slice algebras are equivalent to section algebras when the underlying graph is a line, we generalize this result, showing that slice algebras are always isomorphic to section algebras. Additionally, we examine how the slice algebra's properties change when they are extended to the complete square graph, revealing a duality relationship with previous results on bipartite section algebras. Lastly, we investigate the structure of ideals within slice algebras, particularly those that are toroidal in nature. Nonetheless, we also find that only toroidal slice algebras corresponding to weighted circles possess basic one-dimensional toroidal ideals, which correspond to the weighted circle itself. Consequently, the toroidal slice algebras of complete squares do not possess such ideals. In contrast, the toroidal slice algebras of weighted trees possess no one-dimensional toroidal ideals, unless they are isomorphic to a matrix algebra. Subsequently, the toroidal slice algebras of bipartite graphs, previously studied, do not possess one-dimensional toroidal ideals either, according to our revised understanding. In the process of this research, we found that slice algebras of weighted graphs are completely described as path algebras of weighted graphs, which simplifies the previously proposed classification of section algebras of weighted graphs. Like standard Ramsey interferometry, our findings demonstrate that linear Hadamard gates must be utilized to achieve the optimal performance, corresponding to detecting the real part of the complex amplitude $\Delta\alpha$. This article reviews the current status of sigma term estimates, noting its significance in various areas such as the study of neutrinoless double beta decay, the investigation of in-medium modified pion-nucleon coupling, and the determination of quark mass values. We also examine how lattice QCD has contributed to sigma term estimates, discuss the challenges associated with such computations, particularly in relation to finite volume effects, and examine the different methods used to tackle these challenges. Additionally, we explore the connection between the sigma term and other quantities such as the nucleon mass and the pion-nucleon loop mass. Finally, we highlight the need for further improvements in sigma term estimates, particularly in addressing unresolved issues. One potential path forward involves incorporating an artificial neural network as a new tool for this task. We suggest representing an RGB image as a complex-valued vector that reflects scaling in various colors, thereby capturing a direct relationship between color channels. In doing so, we effectively address many color-related issues that typically require one-dimensional filters in convolutional networks. With this method, we can replace 1D convolutional layers with equivalent 2D convolutions, preventing potential hue shifts and maintaining the original correlation between color values. Additionally, we can represent various types of spectral images, including multi-band datasets like hyperspectral images. Our framework is called SpecCNet and demonstrates specious invariance, which leads to improved performance in multiple semantic segmentation tasks across various domains, including remote sensing, biomedical imaging, and artistic color manipulation. Specifically, SpecCNet achieves state-of-the-art results on the Bethesda 10-band classification dataset and significantly outperforms other methods in the field of hyperspectral image analysis, while requiring fewer parameters. A similar benefit is observed in the Color Name Classification dataset where our method performs competitively while processing images in color space efficiently. Our source code is available at https://github.com/SpecCNet. A video showcasing the method's application is available at https://bit.ly/3k6vQb8. The concept of geometrical scaling, initially observed in deep inelastic scattering and later in (e, e) scattering experiments, can also be applied to the saturation of the gluon distribution, linking the rapidity and xF distributions of hadrons to the saturation scale in the color dipole frame. We demonstrate that this scaling principle provides a unified explanation for the saturation of gluon distribution, connecting deep inelastic scattering, (e, e) scattering, and high-energy hadron interactions. Additionally, we show that geometrical scaling allows us to bridge the gaps between these processes at various energy levels, enabling us to extrapolate from rapidity and xF distributions at current energies to those expected at higher energies, such as in the future Electron-Ion Collider. Such a unified understanding is crucial for exploring the interface between high-energy strong interactions and QCD saturation at small and large x values in the foreseeable future. Furthermore, we observe that geometrical scaling leads to a relationship between the gluon distribution in pPb collisions and the saturation scale in the color dipole frame, as determined from its ratio to the QCD evolution kernel at a specific point x ≈ 10^-5. If this correlation holds, it would result in a non-evolving saturation momentum in pPb collisions at a 25 GeV energy level, which could be verified by the RHIC STAR collaboration. In a related matter, we compare the geometrical scaling of gluon distribution in pPb and p Pb collisions, finding that while they exhibit identical scaling behaviors, their ratios to the QCD evolution kernel display a slight disparity due to a minor difference in the proton's momentum. Ultimately, we find that geometrical scaling offers a versatile tool for analyzing data across various processes and energies, thereby bridging the gaps between them. (Figure adapted from L. Researchers using biased estimators to prepare CMB maps from small camera pictures can expect significant error distributions in strong point sources, which may exceed the noise in the maps. A two-part mathematical framework has been introduced to quantify these errors and establish a link between the CMB map making process and a classical statistical problem known as the "multiple yield Gaussian hypothesis." By considering an input signal that has two components - a pure CMB and a strong point source - and applying a biased estimator, they find that the resulting error is similar to finding the signal's value when its two components are known, which is also a multiple yield Gaussian hypothesis problem. A series of numerical examples, including four that use actual data, demonstrate the effectiveness of this new method for estimating errors in the CMB map making process. The remaining example illustrates an additional advantage of this method over traditional approaches. The code for this entire project can be found on the GitHub platform under the project name "cmb-error."

This alternative method starts with a frequency map that already contains a biased estimate of the CMB, which is known as a biased frequency map. This alternative method is also a multiple yield Gaussian hypothesis problem, which is demonstrated through a series of numerical examples. The paper also shows that the new method for estimating errors in the CMB map making process based on a frequency map is more efficient than traditional approaches and is also more efficient than the first method for estimating errors in the CMB map making process based on a sky map.
