In recent years, Bayesian experiment design based on prior knowledge and posterior update has gained significance, particularly in optimizing inter-sensor frequency ratios for Ramsey measurements. Although Bayesian approaches can outperform adaptive heuristic protocols, they may not effectively utilize information from high-fidelity measurements. This study compares the performance of three methods: (i) Bayesian experiment design with low-fidelity data, (ii) adaptive heuristic optimization with entanglement-basis choice, and (iii) random protocol, across both low- and high-fidelity measurement settings. By directly comparing the information gain from each method, the research finds that Bayesian design remains beneficial for low-fidelity measurements, while entanglement-basis choice can only slightly improve high-fidelity conditions by exploiting already acquired data information. In contrast, random protocol fails to utilize existing data, leading to suboptimal results. This work highlights the advantages of Bayesian design in both low- and high-fidelity Ramsey measurement scenarios, with implications for the implementation of the protocol across different sensor technologies. Furthermore, the study suggests that Bayesian design can be approximated using a population-size-constrained approach, providing a practical implementation strategy. This population-size-constrained method is compared to the random protocol under various population sizes, with the population-size-constrained approach consistently outperforming the random protocol, although less effectively than the full Bayesian design approach. This practical solution to Bayesian design can be used in quantum-driven protocols, paving the way for the deployment of more efficient and low-cost measurement strategies. Finally, the research demonstrates the practical applicability of the population-size-constrained method in optical measurements, with the example of reading out the state of a single photon. By comparing the computational complexity of the population-size-constrained approach to the existing fast adaptive algorithm, the study finds that the population-size-constrained approach achieves comparable computational efficiency, with both methods requiring logarithmic computational time. This computational similarity provides further practical justification for the implementation of the population-size-constrained approach in real-world applications. Overall, the research highlights the significance of Bayesian design, particularly in low-fidelity Ramsey measurements, while also providing a practical and computationally efficient alternative in the population-size-constrained approach. Both methods have the potential to greatly improve the efficiency and accuracy of quantum-driven protocols, particularly in the deployment of quantum technologies. As a result, the population-size-constrained approach provides a valuable solution for the practical implementation of Bayesian design, with the key distinction that the full Bayesian design approach relies on posterior updates, in contrast to the population-size-constrained approach, which requires population-size-only optimization

The Unruh effect, a quantum effect in relativistic time, is typically recognized as a static property. However, we investigate the evolution of quantum states within a time-dependent Lambda system, which represents a universal acceleration, and propose it as a means to detect the timelike Unruh effect. By simulating this model in the laboratory, we believe it may provide a new approach for observing the Unruh effect, ultimately contributing to quantum technology development. In our study, we first derive the densities of states in a time-dependent Lambda system, which exhibit unusual characteristics. By treating the time-dependent Lambda system as a real vector boson field in Minkowski space, we leverage the Fock space and creation/annihilation operators to describe the evolution of quantum states. Subsequently, we establish a set of first-order Heisenberg equations that govern the time evolution of these operators. Using this approach, we develop operator expressions that simulate detection, and calculate the expected detection rates of multiple particles, which can be used to identify the Unruh effect. Notably, we discover that the expected detection rates exhibit distinct logarithmic increases in both thermionic and photomultiplier models as the system's frequency approaches the Planck frequency. To implement this model in the laboratory, we consider an array of three Josephson junctions. By simulating the Josephson junction model, we calculate the expected detection rates using various levels of approximation and verify that the results converge in the high frequency limit. Our simulation indicates that, in the high frequency regime, the expected detection rates exhibit linear relationships with bandwidth. Finally, we propose an experimental setup to observe the Unruh effect. In this setup, we propose an array of numerous Josephson junctions, which can be viewed as a model of a single, complex Lambda system. By simulating this model, we calculate the expected detection rates and demonstrate that the expected detection rates can be increased by two orders of magnitude. Ultimately, we believe that the experimental setup of an array of multiple Josephson junctions has the potential to successfully detect the Unruh effect in the laboratory. Automated Event Extraction has been successfully implemented in English domains such as corporate takeovers and politics, yet this technology remains underdeveloped for non-English languages. Our study presents a Langauge-Agnostic Event extraction framework, evaluating its performance across eight languages while addressing three research inquiries: (a) how does it fare in English and other languages, (b) how does it stack up against existing English models, and (c) how consistent are its predictions across languages. We employed a multi-task learning approach, training our model on English datasets and then testing it on other languages, in an effort to establish a baseline comparison. Notably, our results reveal that this model performs remarkably well in English but struggles significantly outside of this domain. Further investigation showed that this weakness stems from a lack of subject-verb-object coherence in target languages, compounded by complex semantic differences and less reliable text translations. As future work, we recommend developing training data for non-English languages, incorporating multi-source training methods, and exploring the application of transfer learning across related tasks to address this issue. Conditionally, generated text is focused on a specified topic or image. However, conventional methods frequently produce text that is off topic, excessively verbose, or repetitive. Furthermore, they usually lack a clear understanding of how the text relates to the image it's describing. The goal of the MAGIC framework is to address these challenges by creating a system that generates text more intentionally and responsibly. MAGIC introduces three new components that help in this process: first, it places a detailed description of an image at the center of the generation process. Secondly, it uses a set of rules to induce a sense of morality and responsibility in the generated output through specific guidelines. Lastly, it employs structural guidance to frame the generated text in a more logical and organized manner. By applying these methods, MAGIC displays superior performance in producing coherent, contextually relevant, and responsibly crafted text, as demonstrated in its experiments. Furthermore, it maintains greater clarity and conciseness than other existing systems and is capable of generating longer, more extended texts, surpassing prior approaches in this process. A notable application of the framework is its ability to create guidelines for generating text in a responsible and ethical manner, showcasing its effectiveness in this process. A related repository containing the code, datasets, and other supporting materials can be found at https://github.com/astefani/magic. We investigate the simultaneous effects of environmental degradation and Floquet driving on a one-dimensional Bose gas exposed to a cold bath at extremely low temperatures, utilizing the Floquet matrix product density operator method. It is found that the interaction between dissipation and driving, though often thought of as generating heat, can actually facilitate the formation of a Bose-Einstein condensation when the system parameters are carefully adjusted. Moreover, the rate of non-equilibrium heating is found to be highly responsive to the dimensions of the system's Floquet spectrum and can be readily adjusted via the introduction of minimal system anisotropy. The observed phenomenon of enhanced heating rate via Floquet engineering is identified as a universal and potentially valuable tool for experimental and simulation-based studies. Finally, the method developed for calculating non-steady state properties of the Bose gas in the high temperature, long-time limit is discussed, and it is demonstrated that the environment-induced formation of excitations in the system significantly differs from the typical pattern of thermalization observed in closed Floquet systems. This study proposes a hierarchical control strategy comprising leader-follower approaches along with a hysteresis-based hybrid control method to effectively manage a high-voltage low-current DC microgrid. Within the microgrid's power distribution layer, various distributed energy sources and loads are connected in series, making it challenging to achieve stable operation. To address this issue, the proposed approach divides the microgrid into two tiers: a higher-level leader group that implements hybrid control and a lower-level follower group that uses leader-provided setpoints. To ensure smooth power transfer among loads, a power-flow controller in each converter modulates the power and voltage accordingly. We formulate a multi-objective optimization model for the leader group, prioritizing cost, stability, and efficiency over other considerations. To achieve these goals, a multi-layer bi-objective scheduling strategy is developed, incorporating a hybrid approach of robust and stochastic scheduling. To ensure robustness, the leader group implements a robust scheduling strategy, while a stochastic scheduling strategy is employed for loads with uncertain power requirements. To achieve optimal results, a multi-objective optimization model is formulated, incorporating constraints such as power flow, voltage, and control limitations. Following leader-follower strategy implementation, a hybrid control method is proposed, which utilizes hysteresis bands to regulate power and voltage fluctuations. This control strategy enables balanced power flow during transient events, ensuring stable operation of the microgrid. To ensure accurate tracking, the power-flow controller in each converter implements a feedback-based tracking method, utilizing setpoints provided by the leader. With the introduction of hysteresis bands, the controller's tracking accuracy remains unaffected, allowing it to achieve optimal results. The results demonstrate the strategic application of the proposed strategy, showcasing a significant 93.6% reduction in power-flow variations. Additionally, the controller's tracking efficiency is enhanced, resulting in a 99.6% reduction in required power-flow adjustments. To ensure stable operation, the results show a 99.9% reduction in power-flow fluctuations. In conclusion, the proposed strategy presents a novel and effective approach to microgrid power-flow management, utilizing leader-follower control with hybrid microgrid scheduling and hysteresis-based power-flow controllers to achieve optimal results. The unpredictable forces acting on offshore wind turbines, such as turbulence entering through the water and irregular waves, are difficult to model because of their random nature, making it challenging to incorporate into simulations. Due to the complexity of these stochastic factors, precise equations are often used to simulate them for offshore wind turbine applications, assuming the environment can be broken down into separate, independent components with probability distributions that can be accurately defined. However, this simplification can underrepresent the dynamic relationships between individual components, such as wind and waves, especially when considering the water's effect on waves. As a result, this simplification may later affect the accuracy of fatigue life predictions for offshore wind turbines. To address this issue, this research uses a stochastic framework to generate realistic scenarios for atmospheric and wave conditions and assesses how the generated scenarios impact the variability of hydrodynamic forces acting on the turbine. The findings suggest that incorporating stochastic factors significantly increases the variability of hydrodynamic forces compared to a model that does not account for them, resulting in higher expected forces. Furthermore, this increased variability is expected to lead to shorter lifespan predictions for the turbine compared to a model that uses a constant reference velocity. The research also demonstrates the difficulty in achieving consensus among simulations due to the vast number of possible stochastic scenarios, underscoring the importance of incorporating stochastic factors in offshore wind turbine simulations. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to offshore wind turbine research by expanding the scope of environmental modeling, which currently often lacks consideration for stochastic factors. To facilitate the replication of the research's results, all computational models and data are made publicly available. Furthermore, a public release of the code will allow for the simulation of various stochastic scenarios, potentially aiding in the validation and comparison of different stochastic models. By publishing the code in an open-source manner, the research aims to facilitate collaboration among stakeholders in the offshore wind turbine industry. By combining wave and wind data from several databases with advanced processing techniques, this research aims to create a comprehensive understanding of the stochastic environment. Researchers have found that purple leaf-altered Iochroma (a plant in the nightshade family) are actually a misidentified group of Befaria species (also in the nightshade family).  A recent genetic study revealed that OCH-001, previously believed to be Iochroma, is actually Befaria befra, a newly described species discovered through the examination of a collection of Befaria plants. Befaria befra is a unique species found in Peru.  Another species, Befaria purpurea, was also identified and is characterized by its purple leaves.  Befaria species can be distinguished from Iochroma by their smaller flowers and presence of only five stamens.  A key tool for accurately identifying plants is the combination of photographs and genetic data, and is now used in taxonomy.  Interestingly, OCH-001, now Befaria befra, is considered an atypical member of its species complex, and is likely a reproductively isolated individual that originated from a single parent.  Further studies revealed that the evolutionary history of Befaria can be broken down into eight distinct lineages, or clades.  These clades were formed between 1.8 and 5.4 million years ago, and are associated with changes in the Andean mountain range.  A past study incorrectly identified the origins of OCH-001 as either Befaria or Iochroma, and is now considered incorrect. This research explores the potential of Graph Neural Networks to enhance the prediction of travel times. Leveraging GNNs in this context involves representing a network road map as a graph where nodes correspond to locations such as intersections, stops, and destinations, and edges mimic the paths between these nodes. By repeatedly learning from this structured data, a GNN can effectively predict travel times. In this study, multiple GNN variants are compared to conventional solutions such as gradient boosting decision trees. Notably, the proposed approach involves a two-step method where a GNN is used to identify patterns in structured travel time data, which are then fed into a gradient boosting model for prediction purposes. This methodology's efficacy is demonstrated using real-world data from Chicago, Illinois, specifically a dataset provided by Uber ATG – Uber Taxi Graph – containing a subset of the city's road network within a 5-mile radius of Chicago's University Village neighborhood, comprising approximately 348k nodes and 673k edges. Specifically, the research focuses on predicting the estimated time of arrival from the university campus to Wrigley Field. Various GNN variants are tested, including basic models, spatio-temporal graph-based models, and attention-based models. Notably, the attention-based GNN, AGNN, achieved the highest mean absolute error (MAE) reduction of 28.9% when compared to the baseline solution. Furthermore, the study reveals that AGNN outperforms conventional solutions such as gradient boosting decision tree models by as much as 1.4 times, and consistently outperforms other GNN variants. Moreover, the research finds that using Uber ATG's estimated time of arrival from the university campus to Wrigley Field results in an MAE of 3.53 minutes, whereas estimates generated from the dataset used in this study, involving a different driver and vehicle, are 8.12 minutes off the mark. Notably, the estimated travel time as per the actual GPS data is approximately 34.2 minutes. Ultimately, the proposed approach successfully leverages the potential of structured travel time data. To address this challenge, we utilize graph learning methods to assess the influence of well-known actors and actresses. Our method, based on the concept of rich club coefficients, enables us to determine the cooperative effects within a network and pinpoint leaders, ultimately allowing us to create a more accurate movie revenue forecast by incorporating social network characteristics. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of movie characteristics, such as production expenditure, on revenue prediction. We also introduce a novel hybrid forecasting model, combining graph learning and autoregressive integrated moving-average methods, to provide a more in-depth understanding of the complex relationships in the movie industry. When considered in isolation, our proposed methods demonstrate moderate performance, however, the hybrid model exhibits superior predictive capabilities with a significant 0.23 in RMSPE reduction when its output is further refined through autoregressive integrated moving-average methods. When the hybrid model is integrated into existing state-of-the-art forecasting techniques, our results indicate a reduction of 0.058 in RMSPE, a 9.3% improvement. Our research suggests that incorporating star influence and social network features can enhance forecasting precision, particularly when the hybrid model is used in conjunction with other highly accurate methods. We observed that star power is a more consistent predictor of revenue than social club coefficients, indicating a more stable influence of high-profile actors and actresses across different movies. Moreover, our findings reveal a more profound impact of negative connections within the network, suggesting a stronger negative effect of social graph features. Blazars, characterized by their extremely luminous activity, are surrounded by complex astrophysical environments, including winds, jets, and dusty structures, interacting in intricate ways. Studies so far have mainly focused on electron-proton beams within the jets. Recent breakthroughs in observing relativistically moving objects allow us to directly measure polarization in high-energy spectral ranges. A study conducted on the blazar 3C 279, based on its UV/X-ray spectrum, provided an opportunity to investigate polarization in multiple objects using various X-ray telescopes. Findings from observing multiple objects revealed a correlation between polarization and flux, but with a complex pattern, and significant uncertainties in many cases, especially in the polarized flux at zero, thereby hampering the determination of the electron optical depth. Some objects, such as 3C 279, PKS B1510-049, and PKS 0420-37, showed high polarization at their peak flux, but not at lower flux, and in the case of PKS 0420-37, a high level of polarization was recorded. A comprehensive review of theoretical models to explain the observed polarization in the UV/X-ray spectral range has been presented. Polarization in the UV/X-ray spectral range has the potential to provide valuable insights into the properties of blazar jets, particularly their optical depth, and lower energy radiation component. However, the complexity of the environment outside the jet, such as interstellar and intergalactic matter, and various radiation mechanisms, such as Compton scattering, synchrotron radiation, inverse Compton scattering, and reflection, among others, might affect polarization measurements. An investigation into the polarization of reflected radiation in blazars has been proposed, and a detailed discussion on its feasibility has been presented. Additionally, the concept of spectral polarization in the context of reflected radiation has been introduced. A preliminary simulation of polarized reflected radiation in the case of 3C 279 has been conducted using a Monte Carlo method. The simulation of polarized reflected radiation in the case of a blazar has revealed a correlation between its position angle and photon energy, and a level that is several orders of magnitude lower than that of direct radiation. A detailed discussion on the importance of reflected radiation in the context of polarization measurements has been presented, and a call for the development of a Monte Carlo code has been made. An initial version of the code, MC4BLZAR, has been introduced and its capabilities, such as its ability to simulate polarized radiation at various energy levels, have been described

The existence of a primordial magnetic field (PMF) is a plausible explanation for the persistence of isolated magnetic anomalies in the early universe. If present, this field would have been embedded within the differential equations governing the gravitational wave dynamics produced through lensing or collisions, particularly in the gravitational wave frequency band. By simulating and modeling, it's been discovered that a PMF can induce a directional distortion effect on GWs, resulting in a 1-2 order enhancement in the detection likelihood. Notably, the distorted GW frequency spectrum can resemble modal patterns, produced by axion fluctuations predicted in the Axion Isocurve model, which could result in a competition for detection between these signals and the PMF distortion and lensing effects. To counteract this issue, the axial symmetry of the gravitational potential would need to be restrengthened. Existing constraints from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis already impose a limit on the potential magnetic energy density in the frequency band 100-300 GHz, approximately three orders of magnitude above what is theoretically allowed. Consequently, the potential for detecting gravitational waves in this frequency band may be compromised by the possible presence of a PMF. However, the PMF distortion effect on GWs has a predictable pattern and can be amplified; this could be used as a distinctive signature to identify the distortion effect through analysis or data manipulation to compensate for it. By the time 2023's LIGO and Virgo O3 run comes to a close, LIGO and Virgo will likely be able to set a limit on the PMF energy density in the 100-300 GHz frequency band, approximately an order of magnitude tighter than existing current limits. Initial results indicate that deep unsupervised learning offers a superior balance of performance and computational efficiency for this task. However, the reliability of deep learning approaches depends on the quality of training data, which must be optimized using genetic algorithms. This paper proposes a combined deep learning and genetic algorithm approach, where deep neural networks process raw data to generate optimal input for genetic algorithms, which then use this information to maximize the performance of the deep neural networks. This cooperative framework enhances the efficiency of genetic algorithms and improves their ability to learn from the features extracted by deep neural networks. Initial results confirm the success of this approach, showing improved performance and computational efficiency over traditional methods. The application of deep neural networks and genetic algorithms to channel assignment in wireless communication systems, which has been extensively researched using traditional methods, demonstrates the significant advances that deep learning and modern optimization techniques can achieve in this field. In today's world, numerous computer systems can switch between various tasks to improve overall efficiency. Nonetheless, these systems often struggle to adapt quickly to new tasks, and sharing resources among tasks too rapidly can lead to suboptimal performance. To address this issue, we explore different strategies for allocating CPU power in a multitasking system, all of which aim to identify the ideal balance between task switching speed and system performance. Through various experimental methods, we examine the trade-offs between achieving quick task switching and high system performance for both individual tasks and groups of tasks, as well as a new approach that falls somewhere between traditional strategies for improved performance. Our findings suggest that the choice of allocation strategy has a considerable impact on system performance, and that the conventional approach of limiting context switching costs is inadequate in modern systems. To address this problem, we propose a new strategy called 'critical delay' to govern when a new task should be allowed to run, and explored it through different methods of control. Ultimately, we compared the effectiveness of this strategy against other approaches using realistic simulations based on actual system performance. Our results demonstrate that the choice of allocation strategy has a considerable impact on system performance, and that the 'critical delay' approach generally performs better than existing methods, and sometimes even allows all tasks to achieve their optimal performance. However, the 'critical delay' approach does not always outperform other methods in terms of overall system performance, and we provide recommendations for when this strategy might be preferred over alternative approaches. To summarize, our work introduces a new framework for governing CPU allocation in a multitasking system, and explores and compares different strategies for managing multitasking, including their trade-offs and consequences on system performance. To promote the development of new allocation strategies, we have released the underlying simulation framework as an open-source tool, available at https://github.com/tejpant/multitasking-scheduling. Our work also sheds light on the current state of the art in managing multitasking, and highlights areas for further research and development. Ultimately, we hope that the exploration of different strategies and their consequences will inspire the development of better allocation strategies, and contribute to the advancement of the field. The underlying simulation framework is an invaluable resource for testing and evaluating allocation strategies, and we encourage researchers and practitioners to utilize it as a platform for developing and analyzing new strategies, and for conducting comparative analyses of different approaches. Our results provide valuable insights into the trade-offs and consequences of different allocation strategies, and serve as a guide for developers to choose the most suitable approach for specific use cases. A major limitation in bio-inspired robotic systems is often their poor ability to stick to pre-set paths. This problem is particularly prominent in robots learning to hop on soft surfaces. To enhance the system's ability to follow desired trajectories, we've designed a feedback control mechanism. By making adjustments to the actuator torque in real-time, based on the current state of the system, our approach demonstrates superior performance. It was tested in both simulation and physical tests, and was found to track a target frequency of hopping twice as well as a related open-loop strategy. Importantly, our method allows the system to adapt to changes in ground stiffness without needing to modify our approach, and requires minimal training when making adjustments. Overall, our results suggest that our real-time feedback control mechanism is an effective way to improve the system's ability to follow desired trajectories. This could have important implications for related tasks, such as perching or catching an object. For instance, in the long term, our method could potentially allow a system to learn complex tasks on different types of ground, even if it doesn't know its properties. To test this, we also used our approach to study a related task, and found that using real-time feedback control enabled the system to learn to hop on different ground types, despite significant changes to the task requirements. The aim of this research is to transform the validation algorithms for temporal plans into a predictive model that can directly forecast outcomes of task definitions and plan modifications. Developing such a model could streamline the process of creating and refining temporal plans, as well as enable tasks to be optimized pre-emptively. To achieve this, we first examine the underlying logic of a validation algorithm and distill it into a supervised predictive model. Then, we create an implementation of this model in Python and conduct experiments using data derived from the planning domain domain-benchmark suite, specifically focusing on scheduling tasks to enhance battery life. Our results indicate that this model can accurately forecast outcomes in the domain of battery scheduling and other temporal planning domains, including the warehouse domain and the schedule-world domain. Furthermore, we find that this model can successfully predict outcomes of novel unseen task definitions, as well as estimate performance improvements resulting from modified temporal plans. Our implementation and dataset are freely accessible at https://github.com/mweller/planning-forecasting. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the integration of machine learning techniques in temporal planning, similar to recent advancements in reinforcement learning approaches to planning. Experiments on the BLiMP and the BLiMEC datasets reveal that SummScore surpasses existing metrics in evaluating diversity and aligning with human ratings. Overall, our findings suggest that SummScroe can facilitate model comparison and aid in identifying areas for further optimization. Our proposed BEVFusion framework revolutionizes 3D object detection within a LiDAR-based structure by introducing a novel, feature-enhanced fusion approach that drastically improves the current state.  When encountering LiDAR failures, such as those caused by obstructions, the advanced BEVFusion framework significantly outperforms existing methods, including high-ranking ones, by providing a notable increase in performance on the NuScenes and Waymo open datasets. A practical application of this approach can be seen in a controller developed to predict the future state of a robot arm based on a video feed, using a deep neural network. We introduce a novel concept of functorial clustering that addresses a critical issue in its non-functorial counterpart. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various types of data, including finite metric spaces, considering subsets as clusters. For metric data, we establish a method to create a functorial clustering from a functor mapping observations to disjoint subsets. This mapping is subject to a specific condition based on the Hausdorff metric. Our work also explores connections between various linkage methods, including single-linkage, average-linkage, and Ward's method. We prove that certain types of linkages can be viewed as special cases of functorial clustering, and provide conditions under which they can be mapped back to their original forms. Furthermore, we expand the concept of functorial clustering to a broader framework, known as 'k-clustering', which considers the structure of data based on its topological properties. In this context, we establish a method to create a functorial clustering from a functor mapping observations to disjoint subsets based on their k-dimensional metric structure. We also establish a method to create a functor mapping observations to partially ordered sets, which represent the hierarchical clustering of data. These partial orders can be used to reconstruct the original k-clustering data, and we establish conditions under which we can recover the original functor. The goal of semantic parsing is to transform natural language into logical forms by breaking sentences down into meaningful components. Lately, approaches that leverage large amounts of unlabelled data, combined with sophisticated neural models, have shown considerable improvement in state-of-the-art results. It has become essential for these methods to handle few-shot scenarios where the available data is both limited in quantity and absent any explicit annotations. Existing few-shot semantic parsing techniques typically build upon pre-trained models, incorporating data augmentation and categorization to supplement limited training data. They rely on significant amounts of unlabeled data (several million examples) for effective operation. This paper presents an alternative few-shot strategy, adapting existing techniques to function with substantially less unlabeled data (around 17 thousand examples). By merging an attention-based neural model for cross-task attention with an unsupervised pre-training method called Masked Language Modeling, we achieve an impressive result of 81.6% matching performance with an order of magnitude less unlabeled data. This new approach matches the state-of-the-art performance when trained on large datasets under a few-shot setting. Moreover, it outperforms existing techniques both in unsupervised pre-training and few-shot scenarios on the BankData, AirTravel, and Armadillo benchmark datasets. The complex nature of B-type magnetic stars, known as Bp stars, is thought to be responsible for the formation of large magnetospheres and massive disk-shaped structures that surround them. A new hypothesis suggests that these magnetospheres could be the remains of massive disks that formed around 10 to 20 solar masses protostars, rather than being a result of accretion from the star's outer atmosphere as previously believed. By applying this "protostar inheritance" model to the star Ransore/RCV104, we demonstrate that its magnetosphere likely originated from a 10 solar mass protostar, specifically from the disk-shaped structure that formed between 1 to 5 astronomical units. This model allows us to make specific predictions regarding the size and shape of the magnetosphere, resulting in a better fit of the star's mass loss rates and radio emissions during a massive outburst in 2020. This protostar inheritance model can also be applied to other magnetic stars, providing a unified understanding of these objects across various mass ranges from the protostar to the main sequence stage. As a result, it may lead to the discovery of additional candidates with smaller magnetospheres that are currently beyond detection. Ultimately, the protostar inheritance model opens a new window of cross-field research, enabling us to study the early formation of massive stars across X-rays, radio waves, optical light, and gamma rays. Furthermore, it may also allow us to analyze the effects of magnetic fields on massive stars, their disk-shaped structures, and their surroundings using multi-messenger astronomy.

Bass' algorithm (1968) was designed to estimate traffic arriving at a node in a network, but it can be applied more broadly. In automated control, the algorithm's output generates a signal that, when fed back into a dynamic system, leads to equilibrium, demonstrating the algorithm's stabilizing properties. Building on this insight, we explore the algorithm's potential as a control signal itself, showing it can drive a plant's states to a desired target. Theoretical analyses validate the algorithm's effectiveness, demonstrating its ability to withstand minor disruptions and recover quickly from larger-scale attacks. Additionally, we demonstrate how an algorithm modified with a simple correction can ensure the system remains stable under varying conditions, maintaining the controller's integrity and accuracy. The paper includes a detailed discussion on the algorithm's implementation, its connection to traditional control methods, and a step-by-step tutorial for applying Bass' algorithm. Furthermore, a comparative evaluation of Bass' algorithm with established control techniques is presented, illustrating its advantages under specific conditions. The paper also showcases Bass' algorithm in action through two real-world case studies on image recovery. The first examines its ability to repair damaged images from partial information, while the second investigates how this algorithm can assist in 3D image reconstruction. Comprehensive documentation, including code snippets and dataset downloads, are provided to facilitate further research and development. The work includes conversations with David Bass about his algorithm and its broader applications, as well as conversations with Richard Larson regarding extended versions of the algorithm. Overall, this research delves into Bass' algorithm, examining its underlying mathematics, broader implications, and diverse applications, while also highlighting potential untapped areas for further investigation. The study is divided into ten chapters, each focusing on a distinct aspect of Bass' algorithm, including its initial development, theoretical foundation, practical applications, extension, connection to established control methods, capacity for automatic learning, ability to withstand disruptions, recovery from critical failures, utilization in real-world scenarios, and future research opportunities. By systematically evaluating these areas, we seek to determine the current state of Bass' algorithm, identifying areas for further exploration, and uncovering potential future research avenues. Throughout this analysis, we speak with David Bass about his algorithm and its development, as well as discuss potential future research directions with him, Richard Larson regarding an extended version of the algorithm, and other experts in the field. This work introduces an artificial intelligence framework for pathologic stage classification in breast cancer, built using histopathology images and their corresponding clinical labels. A unique dataset was created by combining 50,000 images of breast cancer tissues from patients, along with their corresponding clinical labels and histopathology images. This dataset was used to train a framework called StagingNet, which leverages the powerful classification capabilities of deep neural networks. By testing the framework on a diverse dataset of unlinked patient images, the researchers achieved an impressive 93.5% bicategorical classification performance. Evolution occurs over a long period and is influenced by non-genetic processes such as ecological interactions, which in turn are affected by environmental shifts. However, the relationship between ecological processes and genetic mutation is complex and often overlooked. Traditional theories assume that mutation rates remain constant, whereas environments that adapt and evolve likely experience significant and varied mutations. This paper explores how frequent and random mutations impact ecosystems, particularly those that are highly sensitive to environmental changes. We investigate how easily our speech representation models can be compromised by adversaries using various forms of manipulation, starting from basic attempts using random noise to sophisticated attacks tailored to specific languages and scenarios. Our research sheds light on the effectiveness of several countermeasures, including limitating the model's access to relevant data and retraining it to be more resistant to manipulation. Through a controlled study with human evaluators, we found that adversaries with some knowledge of the target language and scenario can easily create misleading speech representations, both in real-world English speech and a synthetic language designed to trick the model. Even when the representation appears normal to evaluators, the intent behind the speech is often unclear. In contrast, limiting the model's access to relevant data or retraining it using adversarial examples significantly reduces its susceptibility to manipulation. Consequently, we suggest treating speech representation model output as untrusted until properly validated in the future. The code and dataset supporting this research are publicly available at https://github.com/jasonstrausspele/evaluating-speech-representation. By defining a distance metric and an oracle that provides current market prices, we can measure the accuracy of a given AMM and its potential for future surpluses or arbitrage opportunities based on its inherent characteristics. Our findings show that certain AMM designs are more likely to result in higher surpluses, with increased curvature of the pricing curve being a key factor in this regard. For the first time, they analyzed how heavy quarks are distributed among strange and non-strange mesons, both in relation to rapidity and transverse momentum. A key observation was that fragmentation patterns of charm and bottom quarks are similar when considering mesons without strange content. However, this similarity does not hold for mesons containing strange quarks. Moreover, they found that particle distributions of strange and non-strange mesons are related in a way that can be predicted, indicating that the effect of energy and momentum has a universal impact across different types of mesons. This prediction capability also extends to comparing data from proton-lead collisions to proton-proton collisions, revealing similar fragmentation trends. Overall, these analyses provide significant insights into the behavior of heavy quarks when they collide with multiple targets. Furthermore, they found that particle production from these interactions can be accurately described using principles established in fixed-target experiments, thereby validating the concept of rapidity. To explore how API design influences potential misuse, we examined the interfaces 
of three prominent crypto libraries, Python's `cryptography`, `java` and `C` libraries, 
and created a survey to measure how easily each function can be misused by developers.
We analyzed 112 crypto operations from the three libraries, grouping them into 
categories such as hashing, encoding, and encryption, and gathering data from 69 
participants via the survey, along with expert opinions from 10 experienced crypto 
developers. The results showed a significant disparity in the likelihood of misuse, 
ranging between 0% and 55%, with hashing operations being the most prone to misuse and 
encoding operations exhibiting no tendency towards misuse. We found that libraries with 
clear and consistent naming conventions are less susceptible to misuse, and that certain 
groups, such as students and those with less crypto experience, are more likely to misuse 
crypto functions. Additionally, we found common reasons for misuse, including confusion 
between similar functions, overcomplication of the library, and overconfidence in security 
standards. By highlighting these findings and offering best practices for reducing the risk 
of crypto library misuse, our research may help developers and organizations to better 
protect themselves against potential vulnerabilities and improve the security of their 
applications against various types of cyber attacks. As the use of crypto libraries continues 
to grow with applications, studying this risk is becoming increasingly significant. The 
research suggests that educating users about API design and library functionality may be a 
key step in reducing the risk of crypto library misuse. Ultimately, implementing this 
education may serve to improve the overall security and reliability of applications at a

Recent advances in deep learning have significantly boosted the performance of part-of-speech (POS) tagging. However, traditional models are hindered by their inability to effectively handle unknown words. This limitation reduces their practical usefulness in real-world scenarios where word recognition accuracy is critical. Building on the success of set-valued prediction in handling unknown tags, we have developed a set-valued POS tagger that can adapt to words with no training examples. By incorporating a discrete scalar output layer and combining the predictions of dense features and word history, our model achieves a 67.47 tagger accuracy - an enhancement of 2.21% over the baseline tagger. Furthermore, when applied to the chunking task, our proposed tagger also demonstrates superior performance, outperforming the baseline by 3.23% in chunking accuracy. This new approach represents a pioneering effort in developing a tagger that can adapt to unknown words. Additionally, the concept of set-valued prediction may find applications in tackling other neural sequence segmentation and prediction tasks. The source code for this model is publicly available at https://github.com/yu-y Yates/setvalued-pos-tagging. From the dataset released in 2020, our model achieves an average increase of 3.57% in chunking accuracy over the baseline tagger. This research proves the Birkhoff-Kellogg theorem for an arbitrary topological space, 
proving that a sequence of non-expansive mappings converging to a limit mapping 
results in that same limit mapping being a demand function with consistent demand values. 
In this context, a demand function is a set-valued mapping with the property that 
its sequence of values for any fixed point converges to a consistent value as the argument approaches a fixed value. 
A corresponding result is established for the set-valued extension of the Banach fixed-point theorem. 
This approach also enables deriving the Birkhoff-Kellogg theorem for a general metric space. 
Furthermore, it is shown that the theorem does not extend to spaces with non-metric topology. 
Ultimately, these results are applied to analyze the equilibrium prices in cases of multi-stage commodity trade. 
It is found that the equilibrium price is unique in the first two stages but may be countable infinite in the third stage, 
illustrating that the convergence of a sequence of demand functions to a limit demand function does not imply the limit demand function 
is finite, even when the sequence is uniformly convergent. 
In the process, a deeper analysis of the properties of demand functions is undertaken, 
including the definition of consistent demand values and their extension to topological spaces, 
as well as the concept of upper semi-continuity for set-valued mappings in topological spaces. 
Note that the properties of continuous demand functions, 
as studied in the field of mathematical economics, are fundamentally different from those of set-valued mappings studied here. 
In particular, this research is primarily based on the set-valued extension of the Banach fixed-point theorem. 
In the concluding remarks, it is noted that the Banach fixed-point theorem can be viewed as a special instance of the Birkhoff-Kellogg theorem. 
In the case where the topological space is compact, it is shown that the Birkhoff-Kellogg theorem reduces to the Borsuk-Dugundji theorem. 
Finally, it is noted that the Banach fixed-point theorem does not hold for a general metric space; however, it can be proven under the assumption of a complete metric space. 
In the special case where the topological space is compact, it is demonstrated that the Banach fixed-point theorem is equivalent to the Borsuk-Dugundji theorem. 
A distinct notion of demand function is studied in mathematical economics; this concept differs from the set-valued mappings explored

We introduce Visual-guided Texts (ViTa) to refine the visual cues contained within image-classification datasets like CLIP, thereby fostering a more detailed text-image correlation. ViTa pairs each image with multiple captions, each tailored to capture distinct visual aspects, effectively highlighting localized characteristics. This text-image pairing enables CLIP to focus on these subtle visual differences, leading to improved image-classification performance. Notably, this protocol can be seamlessly integrated into the pretraining process of CLIP without requiring further optimization. Notably, the ViTa protocol yields a 2.3% top-1 accuracy gain on the ImageNet database and a 2.8% improvement on the full range of CLIP benchmarks. This performance boost is complemented by a 2.4% image-text alignment increase, as measured by the multiset similarity of CLIP embeddings. Furthermore, ViTa protocols can be made as small as 1 MB or even 0.1 MB without compromising its effectiveness, as evidenced by its robust performance across various image-classification benchmarks. The compatibility of models is a critical consideration when deploying them in real-world settings, including clinical environments. Highdicom is an open-source library that facilitates data interconversion and communication between applications to promote data exchange. With support for widely-used formats such as DICOM, Highdicom enables seamless data transfer between legacy systems and modern machine learning models. Our goal is to extend Highdicom's capabilities to streamline the deployment of deep learning-based diagnostic models operating on imaging data stored in DICOM format. A new highdicom component, called deepdicom, was developed to create a universal plugin for popular deep learning frameworks and medical imaging software, allowing it to interpret model inputs and outputs based on DICOM metadata. This framework was tested using multiple models, including a CT scan-based classifier and an autonomous retinal disease diagnostic system. Our results demonstrate that deepdicom successfully bridges the gap between standard DICOM data and deep learning models, passing a test with over 98% accuracy in the retinal disease diagnosis task. This universal deepdicom plugin for Python medical imaging and machine learning software accelerates model deployment and adoption by eliminating complex data translation hurdles. Additionally, our open-source deepdicom library facilitates data exchange and interoperability, promoting a common standard for medical imaging data communication. A comprehensive, public deepdicom-based dataset was developed, consisting of a large collection of medical images formatted in DICOM and annotated in JSON, named deepdicom-mnist-retina. This work delves into the significance of the SpliceNet model's output, examining whether the characteristics it extracts, known as splice signatures, align with established biological knowledge or research on pre-trained language models. The analysis focuses on the SpliceNet model's performance in DNA classification tasks and its extracted signatures for two SARS-CoV-2 proteins, Spike and Nucleocapsid. It evaluates the similarities between these signatures and existing scientific findings, using various tools and methods for the analysis. The outcomes suggest that the SpliceNet models' extracted features are loosely connected to existing scientific knowledge, raising questions about their potential usefulness in applied biological settings. While the extracted features demonstrate some minor correlations with relevant sequences, the connections are not substantial, and the splice signatures do not offer novel insights for the chosen tasks. In terms of task performance, the SpliceNet models' results are mixed; for the DNA classification task, they perform moderately well compared to a random forest baseline but poorly for the Spike protein classification task, failing to surpass a simple baseline model. The limited performance of the SpliceNet models on the Spike protein classification task suggests that the learned features may not be useful for tasks involving sequence-level annotations, casting doubt on the suitability of the SpliceNet models for the classification of protein sequences. Overall, the findings raise doubts about the practical utility of the SpliceNet models in real-world biological domains. We've created a class of integrators for solving Hamilton's equations on coadjoint orbits, ensuring the preservation of crucial structural elements even when discretized. Called collective Lie-Poisson integrators, they utilize modified versions of integrals such as Casimirs and coadjoint orbits, resulting in simplified forms that maintain key characteristics. A fundamental discretization method, the Euler-Lagrange scheme, is adapted from analogous continuous flows, and custom integrators are developed using a novel approach that combines geometric and numerical techniques. Comprehensive analysis validates the performance of these new discretizers, which outperform standard methods like Runge-Kutta in preserving key orbital properties. Notably, a detailed examination of their application to the restricted Vlasov-Poisson system reveals improved retention of Casimirs and orbital characteristics. Extensive numerical results confirm the proposed discretizers' ability to maintain key invariants and provide accurate approximations of key observables, such as actions, angular momentum, and orbital positions, with high precision and minimal error. Furthermore, these new discretizers exhibit superior qualities in applications such as restricted Vlasov-Poisson equations and the Euler-Poisson equations, particularly when combined with other specialized methods, like symplectic andshrink-filters. Ultimately, the performance of these new discretizers is comparable to, or in some cases, superior to state-of-the-art methods like Runge-Kutta and Verlet method. As such, the collective Lie-Poisson integrators presented here represent an advanced and efficient addition to the toolkit of numerical analysts and physicists. We conducted a study using daily microlensing sampling data from the OGLE-2016b and OGLE-2016e campaigns to explore discovered and unexplored planet distributions. Despite limited discoveries in the general OGLE-2016e campaign, we found a notable planet with a mass ratio of $2.1\times10^{-4}$ that was initially uncovered through pilot sampling data. By analyzing these discoveries within various discovery methods, we found that pilot sampling data yielded a higher number of low-mass ratio planet detections compared to the main campaign. Unanticipated microlensing planert discoveries in the OGLE-2016e campaign further strengthened this pattern. Ultimately, we believe pilot sampling data can better reveal planets with low mass ratios in microlensing events. Additionally, we observed an uneven planet sub-spaces distribution, which led to the detection of planets with mass ratios exceeding $10^{-4}$. However, these high-ratio planets were largely overlooked in the OGLE-2016e and 2016b campaigns, suggesting future investments should focus on surveys with extensive coverage of blue optical photometry to recover these elusive planets. Lastly, we identified an underexplored planet property space in both microlensing and transit methods, presenting an opportunity for future investigations to shed light on this overlooked area.

We introduce Landmark Gabor Filters, a novel image representation method that
integrates distinct Gabor filters tied to equivalent visual properties. The local
output of these filters serves as robust, formative image features, which are
described as being orientation-independent. Landmark Gabor Filters have the
capability to enhance representation robustness against various orientation
changes by collectively encoding unique visual characteristics. Building on this
concept, we develop a novel image description approach, referred to as LGF-DAA,
which leverages multiple translation-invariant features to dynamically determine
the significance of each feature through adaptation. Experimental findings indicate
that LGF-DAA outperforms existing feature fusion strategies in automatic image
description, also achieving consistent results when dealing with image
localization tasks. Additionally, our analysis of the obtained features
demonstrates the unique properties of each Gabor filter, contributing to the
existing research in image description. The proposed LGF-DAA method
significantly improves precision over current state-of-the-art image description
methods, including the top-ranked Fusion and Im2Calcref approaches. Further
details on the project can be found at https://s107.github.io/LGF-DAA/. The
project's code and necessary datasets have been made accessible through the
GitHub repository at https://github.com/s107/LGF-DAA. We have successfully
obtained the CUREC research ethics approval number 2020-ERI-02. Finally, our
research data are accessible for review at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cviu.2021.02.003.

When conducting a rank correlation analysis, p-value estimates are typically derived under the assumption of a bivariate normal distribution of data. However, when this assumption is violated, p-value estimates become unreliable, with actual error rates potentially being lower than claimed ones. To address this issue in non-normal data sets, we employ a non-parametric p-value estimation method. This approach involves using nearest neighbor estimation in a bivariate data space to estimate p-value distributions. Unlike other non-parametric methods that rely on asymptotic approximations, our method offers accurate p-value estimates based on finite sample sizes. Our comparative analysis reveals that this method is more reliable than p-value estimates based on bivariate normal assumptions, especially in cases involving skewness and outliers. Furthermore, when comparing this non-parametric method to a Bayesian approach, we found that the former tends to yield type I error rates similar to those of the Bayesian method, but at a significantly lower computational cost. Our results suggest that the non-parametric method can be a suitable alternative to the Bayesian approach, especially in cases involving large data sets and limited computational resources. When dealing with small data sets, however, the Bayesian method may offer a superior solution due to its ability to incorporate prior knowledge and achieve convergence at a faster rate. This study diverges from this approach, instead examining whether localized feedback can also be an effective tool for stabilization. To address this question, we focus on a specific scenario - the linear batchelor vortex flow. When this flow becomes unstable, it demonstrates two types of transitions, known as Hopf bifurcation and pitchfork bifurcation. Our study shows that localized actuation, when applied in a specific manner through the entire flow domain, can be used to stabilize both types of transitions. Importantly, we found that two spatially localized controls, when applied at specific locations and with adjusted phases, also have stabilizing effects. This discovery reveals that localized feedback can be an effective means of stabilizing fluid flows. We have also developed a theoretical framework to explain the conditions necessary for stabilization and identified key parameters that contribute to this effect. This study provides a valuable framework for the design and implementation of localized actuation strategies in engineering applications aimed at stabilizing fluid flows. Furthermore, we believe that this work may pave the way for the development of new strategies in fields like medicine and biology, where the manipulation of fluid flows has practical applications. To facilitate the design of optimized actuation schemes, we have created a open-access software package, named L2F, which can be used to replicate our findings and design actuation strategies for a variety of physical systems. Additionally, we have contributed a detailed description of the local2f library, which was developed in this study. Local2F is an open-source Python library that is designed to assist in the local2F project. It consists of two primary components: the first is responsible for generating actuation schemes, while the second simulates the resulting dynamics. Through an example-based approach, we demonstrate the benefits of using local2F for the efficient design of local actuation schemes. Furthermore, we leverage local2F's capabilities to explore higher-order effects in the context of the bifurcation analysis of the batchelor vortex flow. One notable outcome of this investigation is the identification of a secondary pitchfork bifurcation associated with a higher-order mode in the y-direction. This discovery reveals that this mode interacts with lower-order modes near the primary pitchfork bifurcation, leading to the creation of a mixed mode that contributes to the stabilization strategy. While explanations can enhance end-user trust in recommender systems, relying on post-hoc explanations for these models may undermine their model's reliability. This is because these explanations often lack a direct connection to the primary recommendation model. In this study, a transparent recommender model called ATARS is introduced, incorporating a self-explanatory module that integrates user and item features within an attention-based framework. By integrating this module, ATARS generates self-explanatory key values, or explanation tokens, that are incorporated into the prediction process. The research indicates that ATARS generates explanations that closely align with actual item characteristics, and that using these explanations leads to improved model generalizability and user engagement. Notably, comparisons show that ATARS surpasses other explanation-based recommender models, including one by Tang et al. [1], which was inspired by the external validity theory in social science. Compared to an state-of-the-art recommender model known as PGAR, ATARS achieves a significant 2.0% increase in generalizability, according to evaluations on real-world datasets. The researchers also conducted eye-tracking studies and gathered user feedback via online surveys and interviews, revealing that users prefer the explanations generated by ATARS and that these explanations lead to increased user satisfaction with the system. The findings suggest that incorporating explanations can improve the trustworthiness of recommender systems, and that a transparent recommender like ATARS is well-suited for environments that demand explainability, reliability, and user satisfaction. The source code for ATARS will be made available upon acceptance of this work.

Our research highlights various distribution families where sample complexity is directly influenced by the query radius. Specifically, we've identified three concept classes where double sampling is reliable with relatively few examples: (1) the cover set family, (2) the dilated lattice body family, and (3) the ellipsoid family. Our results validate theoretical predictions while also demonstrating them through practically achievable distribution-free robust learning methods based on doubly smoothed k-nearest neighbor estimation. Our findings provide significant insights at multiple scales of uncertainty. Furthermore, we've established lower bounds on the number of required examples by leveraging sharp contrasts, thereby confirming that our findings are nearly optimal. These results are based on a novel double sampling contrast which allows us to analyze distribution-free robust learning in a more efficient manner. Our research also provides new insights into the complexity of distribution-free learning, revealing that some robust double sampling problems may be harder than others. For instance, we've shown that learning convex body properties in the ellipsoid family, an inherently challenging task, may have a sample complexity escalation, contrary to the findings in the dilated lattice body family. Our research is a testament to the effectiveness of doubly smoothed techniques in robust learning, providing significant advancements to the field. The scalability of model predictive control has become a significant concern due to its widespread application across disciplines.  One method for improving control efficiency without increasing computational demands is by incorporating the Koopman operator framework, which has been explored primarily in academic settings.  This discussion will center on control within large-scale networks of interconnected agents, applying the Koopman operator framework to improve model predictive control.  By utilizing the Koopman operator framework, the time-consuming iterative convergence in model predictive control can be minimized.  Several key properties and advantages of using the Koopman operator framework in model predictive control will be discussed, despite evidence suggesting time-varying Koopman operators do not lend themselves well to off-the-shelf optimization techniques.  This discussion will provide an in-depth analysis of using the Koopman operator framework in model predictive control, highlighting its benefits and limitations while exploring avenues for further research.  Ultimately, the discussion will yield a concise, algorithmic approach incorporating the Koopman operator framework, which improves convergence time over traditional model predictive control. modelling it as a Markov process with transition probability matrix P. 
By treating the matrix exponential as a sum of exponentials with eigenvalues 
as coefficients, we find the eigenvalues of P by solving a polynomial equation 
related to its trace. This approach yields a formula for the characteristic 
polynomial of P based on symmetries in the matrix, and we present a formula 
for its evaluation. This allows us to express the matrix determinant, 
permanent, and other multi-linear functions of P through the characteristic 
polynomial, along with novel expressions for P's rank and non-zero off-diagonal 
elements. This method is particularly efficient for large n and small n, and it 
enables us to extend its applicability to the bivariate random walk on a cylinder 
and other related models. These results are confirmed by numerical tests and 
the associated open-source code is shared. Finally, we explore an analogous 
approach for the tri- and quad-variate random walks on corresponding surfaces. 
However, due to computational complexity, we present only the bipersonal case.

Gravitational modules in code such as N-body tools (e.g., MultiPhenom, GAlgebra) and Farooq rely on the Fast Multipole Method (FMM), allowing for efficient computation of far-field interactions in astrophysical simulations. N-body tools utilize the C++ implementation of FMM in the HipsterLib library, further developing it with additional features. This integration is presently applied in both Phenom 30G simulations and observations with the Farooq telescope, a 10m optical instrument for verifying the Standard Model of cosmology through verification of the Cosmic Inflation Signal. This research initiates a series of studies aimed at analyzing the HipsterLib library's implementation of FMM, including its timing analysis, validation against the CPU-based library for 2nd-order Spectral Expansion of FMM (S2E-FMM), and an investigation into potential uses of accelerated multi-pole methods in future cosmological observations. 

In this research, we compare the computational performance of multi-threaded HipsterLib implementations on GPUs and CPUs for tasks involving S2E-FMM and the accelerated multi-pole method in a scenario where the latter method uses either S2E-FMM or as a black-box alternative to FMM for log(1/K^2) terms. This research assesses the potential for further optimization by utilizing the full potential of parallel processing for tasks involving these libraries and explores the efficacy of replacing traditional recursive algorithms with iterative alternatives within S2E-FMM.

We introduce an augmented policy cloning method called Augmented Matching Policy Cloning, which enables us to isolate the student's learning style when taking cues from an expert. This technique allows us to effectively transfer a teacher's behavior to a student in complex control problems with numerous variables. By comparing the performance of our method with conventional policy cloning, we find that it significantly improves the ability of a student policy to mimic an expert policy. Furthermore, when the student interacts with its environment, it surpasses the expert in performance due to its unique learning style, which can be leveraged to enhance problem-solving capabilities. These findings suggest that distinct learning styles can be identified, analyzed, and optimized, which could have important implications. Based on these results, we propose two potential research directions: one that involves decomposing complex policies into their constituent learning styles, and another that involves integrating these styles in order to expedite the development of policies that effectively interact with dynamic environments. These styles could potentially be used as teaching tools, which could lead to the development of mentor policies that are tailored to the needs of students with unique learning styles. Additionally, we provide an initial framework for systematically evaluating the various styles that underlie policy behavior, which can be expanded to include a broader range of features and policy types.

Recent advancements in resonant spin maser research have led to notable improvements in their performance, particularly with the implementation of digital signal processing techniques. This paper will explore the concept of digital signal processing within resonant spin maser frameworks, focusing on the potential for further optimization through advanced control methods. By integrating various signal processing techniques, it is possible to enhance various parameters such as the maser's spectral purity, low-frequency sensitivity, time stability, and detection sensitivity for minute magnetic field changes. Key methods for achieving this integration involve leveraging complex amplitude and phase modulation, multiple-state excitation techniques, and advanced methods for analyzing resonator signals. Additionally, the use of specialized algorithms can further refine parameters like spectral purity and low-frequency sensitivity, while excitation methods can improve detection capabilities. Ultimately, the potential exists for significant enhancements to the performance of resonant spin maser systems through the incorporation of digital signal processing and innovative control strategies. This work also highlights the unique potential of these systems for making highly accurate measurements of nuclear magnetic resonance and electronic paramagnetic resonance, as well as for developing extremely sensitive detectors of low-frequency magnetic fields and matter at the quantum level. Furthermore, the principles behind the resonant spin maser have been successfully applied in a new type of optical device known as the optical spin maser. This system utilizes a complex network of optical fibers and lasers to amplify a specific, isolated photon signal, demonstrating the possibility of coherent single-photon generation. This optical spin maser has the potential for use in highly secure quantum communication systems, with current research focused on further enhancing its performance and operational capabilities. This research is being carried out using a hybrid optical fiber and solid-state architecture. Initial test results have shown that a large portion of the available laser power can be achieved with a relatively low number of optical fibers. This is an important factor, as a smaller number of fibers correspond to a larger loss of coherence. However, the current design also suffers from limitations in the maser's frequency range and operational stability due to the use of a laser source. This restriction can be overcome by utilizing a more advanced, self-contained system that incorporates a semiconductor diode pump source. This system has the potential for use in a new type of secure quantum communication system, with the ability to generate multiple, indistinguishable photons at a high rate. This optical spin maser is an innovative device that combines elements of resonant spin and optical systems, with the potential for use in highly secure quantum communication systems, efficient light sources, and light manipulation schemes. Researchers have been studying how to express graphical properties through polynomial equations, and some have focused on surface embeddings as their area of inquiry. A key factor in understanding these embeddings is a graph's genus, which indicates its minimal surface embedding. A new method has been proposed to determine a graph's genus using polynomial equations, specifically a set of equations based on a particular arrangement of faces and edges. To test the effectiveness of this approach, the method was applied to stars, which are graphs defined by connecting a central point to multiple peripheral points. Analysis using the proposed technique revealed some distinct characteristics of polynomial equations representing the genus of a graph, such as specific factors and degree relationships. Furthermore, the method was used to examine the genus of certain graph families and to analyze how the genus changes when these graphs are modified. A key finding was that, under certain conditions, the genus of a graph family decreases or remains the same after an operation called contraction. To further explore the potential of this method, the study investigated whether, for any graph family, there exists a simpler set of polynomial equations representing its genus compared to the initial set. A theoretical demonstration of this idea was provided using the example of a family of cubes. Additionally, the method was applied to examine relationships between surface embeddings and another graph characteristic called girth. The results suggest that, given a graph's girth, it becomes possible to express further surface embedding properties through polynomial equations. This study investigates how communication can be further reduced in stochastic optimization techniques by analyzing the potential of the gradient through time-varying adaptive methods. Given that these methods already offer superior performance with reduced communications, we develop a strategy that estimates potential using past data, thereby eliminating the need for current data communications. By adapting this concept to specific, complex functions, we create a new algorithm that achieves reduced communications while maintaining fast convergence rates. Moreover, this approach can be applied to various optimization problems by modifying the estimation strategy, and it is incorporated into a novel method called await. We assess the effectiveness of await on large-scale problems, including linear regression and empirical risk minimization in machine learning and clustering, and provide numerical evidence of its superior performance compared to standard methods. A key benefit of await is its ability to achieve faster convergence on large clusters, and theoretical convergence rates for await are confirmed using analysis and optimization theorems. Further, we develop a variant of await without assuming bounded domains and extend it to distributed stochastic optimization, resulting in a method that reduces communications between parallel processing units. await is implemented using Python and CUDA, and its potential applications include large-scale problems in logistic regression, matrix factorization, and clustering. The source code is available online. [This is an extended version of a paper that appeared in the proceedings of ICML 2019.] As an added benefit, await offers performance and communication improvements over other adaptive methods, and it is proven to have a lower overall cost. This is because await estimates potential using the information potential analysis of Vercautren and Glineur, and it is applied to specific, complex functions. While numerous NLP applications have demonstrated the potential of transfer learning, limited research has been conducted to explore its efficacy and efficiency in similar tasks across related languages. In this research, we have investigated the cross-lingual transfer capabilities of state-of-the-art English models when applied to tasks in German and other Germanic languages, including Dutch, Frisian, and Scandinavian languages. Our findings indicate that transfer learning significantly enhances model performance when adapting to tasks in languages that share a common origin with English. Notably, our results show that zero-shot transfer is a promising area for further exploration, as three out of five languages in this category achieved satisfactory performance. Meanwhile, our data suggest that transfer learning has a positive impact on task performance, particularly in languages that are further removed from English linguistically. Interestingly, our observations suggest that task-specific models often excel over pre-trained models, except in the case of English-related tasks. Our research also reveals that the size and the level of annotation in each language significantly affect the performance gain resulting from transfer learning. Finally, our analysis reveals that the differences in performance among English models are relatively minimal when adapted to German, whereas they become more pronounced as the linguistic distance from English increases. Our findings are consistent across two popular evaluation metrics, prompting and ranking. Based on these conclusions, we recommend task-agnostic pre-trained models with strong performance on English as the initial model to adapt to tasks in languages that share a common origin with English.
